1020-sword-blades-and-poppy-seed:
Amy Lowell, an American poet and force behind Imagism, fills this book with sharp, bright pictures: gardens, smoke, music, and city streets, each caught in a few hard lines. The title pairs war's steel with the poppy's sleep, and the poems swing between clash and calm.

Lowell borrows from Japanese forms and from free verse, letting image lead and meter follow. Some poems tell small tales; others simply set a scene and let it glow. The book shows her at her most daring, and it gives a fine entry to the new poetry of the 1910s.
10370-sustained-honor-the-age-of-liberty:
John R. Musick published this historical romance in 1909, as volume ten of his Real America in Romance series. Its subtitle, The Age of Liberty Established, marks the turn from revolt to a settled American freedom. Musick argues that plain details of daily life make history truer than stiff, formal chronicles alone.

Fiction, he says, arranges facts from nature and experience into new but natural scenes, so readers feel the past. This volume treats the remote and direct causes of liberty taking root. Readers get a vivid, period tale of the Revolution's aftermath, full of character and custom.
10632-the-healthy-life-cook-book-2d-ed:
Florence Daniel's The Healthy Life Cook Book, in its second edition of 1915, is a guide to plain, nourishing everyday eating. It grew out of the health-food movement of its day, which favored simple foods over rich, heavy fare. Recipes and advice aim at fitness that lasts through workdays, Sundays, and holidays alike.

The book favors whole grains, simple porridges, and honest home cooking in place of white bread, pastries, and sloppy, hard-to-digest dishes. Its tone is practical and encouraging, written for households rather than trained cooks. Modern readers get both usable recipes and a clear picture of how Edwardian reformers thought about food and health.
10676-the-reign-of-greed:
Jose Rizal's El Filibusterismo, his second novel of Philippine life, appears here in Charles Derbyshire's complete English version, The Reign of Greed, published in Manila in 1912. Written a few years after Noli Me Tangere, it looks at the last days of Spanish rule in the islands in a graver, less hopeful tone. Rizal had grown discouraged in his efforts to win reform by peaceful means.

The novel follows students, officials, friars, and plotters through a colony choked by greed and fear, toward a dark reckoning. Its dedication to three executed priests had helped bring Rizal himself to trial and death in 1896. Readers get a central work of Philippine literature and a key text of anti-colonial thought.
10809-why-we-are-at-war-2nd-edition-revi:
Members of the Oxford Faculty of Modern History wrote Why We Are at War in 1914 to set out Great Britain's case at the outbreak of the First World War. The revised second edition adds documents, including the authorized English translation of Germany's White Book and the Russian Orange Book. Chapters treat Belgian and Luxemburg neutrality, the growth of alliances, and the race of armaments since 1871.

The authors argue from treaties, above all the 1839 treaty guarding Belgium, that Britain entered war for law and small nations. The book is both argument and source collection. Readers get the British academic case for war, as it was made in the first months of fighting.
10839-sugar-and-spice-comical-tales-comi:
James Johnson's Sugar and Spice, published by Dean and Son of Fleet Street, offers comical tales comically dressed for children. The opening verses tell of dear children giving a party with no grown person there, laughing heartily without a servant's care. Lots are cast for who must play servant, and the lot falls on T. Good.

T. Good will not come when rung or called, till coaxed with marmalade to take a letter out, protesting he was scarcely made to post and run about. The verses keep that playful tone throughout. Young readers get rhymed nonsense and fun, in a bright Victorian children's book.
10886-the-untamed:
Max Brand published The Untamed in 1919, a Western of the desert, the panther, and the phantom rider. Its thirty-eight chapters run from "Pan of the Desert" and "The Panther" through "Silent Shoots," "The Mute Messenger," and "Whistling Dan, Desperado," to "The Song of the Untamed" and "Death." Black Bart, the panther's paw, and the wild geese haunt the tale.

Brand writes of lone riders, rescues, long rides, and a hero more wild than tame, with speed and color. The novel helped make his name in pulp fiction. Western fans get a classic of the genre, fierce, romantic, and swiftly told.
10949-the-romance-of-zion-chapel-3d-ed:
Richard Le Gallienne set this 1898 novel in a sooty provincial town, where Zion Chapel and its minister shape local life. Eli Moggridge, a Nonconformist preacher with new ideas, meets Jenny, Theophil, and Isabel in a story of art, faith, and love. A literary society, a Morris wallpaper craze, and a chapel renaissance stir the town's narrow streets.

Jenny's love and death, and Theophil's life afterwards, give the novel its emotional centre, while Le Gallienne pokes gentle fun at chapel respectability. The book blends romance with social comedy, praising beauty and sincerity against dull convention. Readers get both a love story and a portrait of English chapel culture at the end of the nineteenth century.
10997-the-world-of-waters-or-a-peaceful-:
Mrs. David Osborne wrote this 1852 geography book as a peaceful voyage around the world's waters, told through the Wilton family and their friends. Chapters sail from the Mediterranean and Adriatic to the North Sea and Baltic, then to the Caspian, the Red Sea, and the seas of Asia, and on to Greenland, Hudson's Bay.

Dialogues explain whales and their oil, with a sperm whale yielding as much as 120 barrels, flying fish, monsoons, and the aurora borealis, while stories of wrecks, slave ships. Illustrations picture tropical scenes. The book teaches geography, natural history, and moral reflection together, in the manner of Victorian family reading.
11074-the-damned:
Algernon Blackwood wrote this 1914 supernatural novel about a brother and sister visiting a country mansion. Bill, over forty and set in his ways, agrees to a month's visit to Mrs. Franklyn, a banker's widow, because the house offers a fine library, an organ, a quiet workroom, and perfect service. His sister Frances hopes the visit will cheer them both.

The house itself, altered by the late banker and as bare as a museum wing, soon weighs on Bill's mind. Visions of Mabel, his hostess, sinking into depths of fire and blood, and a garden standing at attention at dusk, suggest a place haunted by past suffering. Blackwood builds dread slowly, through atmosphere rather than shocks, and the novel remains a classic of psychological ghost fiction.
11089-the-education-of-the-negro-prior-t:
Carter G. Woodson wrote this 1919 history of Black education in America from the beginning of slavery to the Civil War. Chapters move from religion with letters, through education as a right of man, to actual schooling, better beginnings, urban education, reaction, religion without letters, and learning in spite of opposition. Higher education, vocational training, and public expense close the study.

Woodson shows clergymen as the first educators, teaching enslaved people to read scripture, and planters who favoured gospel teaching as a defence of slavery. Later, free Black people in the Northwest seized schooling so eagerly that their progress disproved claims of incapacity. Documents, bibliography, and index support the text. The book remains a foundational work in African American history.
11116-the-wonderful-bed:
Gertrude Knevels wrote this 1912 children's fantasy about Rudolf, Ann, and Peter, staying alone at Aunt Jane's without their mother. In a big, creepy nursery, wind howling and rain beating the panes, the children dread the great old four-poster bed, hung with faded chintz and almost touching the ceiling.

Aunt Jane's old toys lead to dreams: an angry warming pan, a visit to a goose, a false hare, real live pirates aboard the Merry Mouser, Catnip Island, mutiny, Captain Jinks. Emily Hall Chamberlin illustrated the book. Knevels writes a cosy, imaginative bedtime adventure, where a strange bed becomes a doorway to dreamlands.
11377-the-man-whom-the-trees-loved:
Algernon Blackwood's 1912 tale The Man Whom the Trees Loved concerns a painter who paints trees by a special divining instinct for their essential qualities. He knows why no two beeches are alike, and catches a tree's individuality as others catch a horse's, though he never had lessons and his drawing is often wildly inaccurate. Flowers, landscapes, people, and animals defeat him; trees emerge alive beneath his brush, shining, frowning, or dreaming.

Old David Bittacy, late of the Woods and Forests, pays twenty guineas and feels he can hear a painted tree rustle. Blackwood's story turns that love uncanny, as trees seem to claim the painter. It remains a classic of weird fiction, quiet rather than violent, and rooted in forest atmosphere.
11403-the-churches-of-coventry-a-short-h:
Frederic W. Woodhouse's 1909 Churches of Coventry, with forty illustrations, gives a short history of the city and its medieval remains. Contents cover the monastery and city, the priory and cathedral ruins, St. Michael's church in history, exterior, and interior, Holy Trinity church in the same three parts, St. John Baptist's, Grey Friars, White Friars, St. Mary Hall, and the Carthusian monastery. A frontispiece shows Coventry's three spires.

Woodhouse writes for visitors and local readers, combining dates with description of stonework, porches, and towers. The book preserves Coventry's churches as they stood before later destruction, making it a valuable record. Its illustrations help readers follow the text church by church.
11505-all-things-considered:
G. K. Chesterton's essays, first published in 1908 and reprinted in 1915, take up flying subjects of the day and treat them as serious matter. Titles run from cockneys and their jokes, the fallacy of success, and running after one's hat, to patriotism and sport, French and English ways, and the Zola controversy.

Chesterton warns lovers of serious literature to keep clear, calling the pieces crude and shapeless papers on current themes. The charm lies in that very roughness: a sharp mind turning a small topic, a limerick, or a London street into an argument about how people live.
12056-phases-of-faith-or-passages-from-t:
Francis William Newman's 1874 book Phases of Faith, or Passages from the History of My Creed, opens with a preface to the first edition. In it, Newman calls the book perhaps egotistical, certainly so in form, yet not in purport and essence. Personal reasons, he writes, cannot wholly be disowned for desiring to explain himself to more than a few who, on religious grounds, are unjustly alienated from him.

Newman traces his own movement through religious positions, from evangelical belief to a freer, more questioning faith, driven by conscience and by curiosity about truth. The book became a classic Victorian spiritual autobiography, read alongside his brother John Henry Newman's Apologia, as a record of how one serious mind changed its creed and lived with the change.
12223-the-idler-volume-iii-issue-xiii-fe:
The February 1893 number of The Idler, volume three, issue thirteen, was edited by Jerome K. Jerome and Robert Barr for Chatto and Windus. The Idler was an illustrated monthly for leisure reading, mixing fiction, humor, and interviews.

Contents include I. Zangwill Cheating the Gallows, M. E. Braddon on her first novel The Trail of the Serpent, Jerome Novel Notes, William Canton The Skater, and Archibald Forbes My Servant Andreas. Forbes farewell to Andreas, with a father watch and a lump in the throat, gives the number its emotional center. The issue shows late Victorian magazine culture at ease: famous names, short fiction, and talk of books for readers with an hour to spare.
12300-the-true-george-washington-10th-ed:
Paul Leicester Ford published The True George Washington in 1896, reaching a tenth edition with J. B. Lippincott. Ford, editor of Jefferson writings and Poor Richard sayings, aimed to show Washington as he was, neither marble saint nor villain.

Ford quotes Washington own admission of foibles and Shakespeare plea to speak of me as I am. Chapters follow Washington youth, surveying, soldiering, farming, and presidency, with a mid-book scene of neighbors gathering at ordinaries, clubbing to share punch and wine. Ford stresses Washington temper, ambition, and self-control. The book was a popular corrective to hero worship, and it remains a readable life built from letters and records.
12431-the-coquette-or-the-history-of-eli:
The Coquette, or The History of Eliza Wharton, founded on fact and written by a lady of Massachusetts, tells of a young woman famed for wit and charm. A historical preface, with a memoir of the author, warns that lifting the veil between real and ideal needs a tender heart and a gentle hand. The novel draws on actual personages.

Eliza, courted, admired and judged, moves through letters and society toward a fall that made the book a moral warning. The novel, in epistolary form, lets suitors, friends and family speak for themselves. It remains a classic early American tale of reputation, love and choice, and of the price a woman paid for freedom in a strict age.
1277-melmoth-reconciled:
Honoré de Balzac takes up the legend of Melmoth, the man who sold his soul for long life, and gives it a Parisian twist. A cashier, ruined by debt, meets Melmoth and takes the bargain. He soon finds that a soul no one will buy is a curse, not a prize.

The tale moves through counting houses and salons, where Balzac shows money as the true devil of modern life. The story is short, sharp, and grimly funny. It suits readers who like Balzac's Paris and a devil's bargain told with a banker's eye.
12779-helen-with-the-high-hand-2nd-ed:
Arnold Bennett called Helen with the High Hand an idyllic diversion, and the comedy suits the label. Helen returns to the Potteries town of Bursley after time away, and finds her family buzzing. Her younger sister Lilian, once a girl with a ribbon in her hair, is now eighteen and engaged to Andrew Dean. Gossip, pride, and old affection tangle.

Helen, sharp and high-handed in the best sense, manages relations with a firm, amused touch. Bennett sets the tale among the Five Towns streets and homes he knew so well. The novel offers light, witty domestic comedy with a heroine who knows her own mind.
13064-persia-revisited:
General Sir Thomas Edward Gordon, former military attaché at Tehran, published Persia Revisited in 1896 after a return trip in 1895. His route runs from London to Baku, across the Caspian, and into Persia, with notes on oil wells, steamers, salmon, and the Enzelli lagoon. Later chapters cover the late Shah's reign, camp life, the tobacco strike of 1891, and the new Shah, Mozuffer-ed-Din.

Gordon notes the Martini-Henry rifle, called the Marteen, now common in private hands, with brass cases reloaded again and again. He also retells a tale of Nadir Shah, who claimed descent from the sword for seventy generations, not seven. The book is a soldier-diplomat's report, useful for trade, arms, and court life in late Qajar Persia.
13197-wear-and-tear-or-hints-for-the-ove:
S. Weir Mitchell, a Philadelphia doctor and president of the College of Physicians, published Wear and Tear in a fifth, revised edition after first writing it fifteen years earlier. Mitchell warns a restless nation, tempted by vast chances, against working brain and body past their powers. His preface notes how fast dress, diet, schooling, and daily habits had changed.

Mitchell argues that every organ must take its turn of work and rest, so blood can nourish each part in turn. He blames nervous illness in crowded towns on steady mental strain, poor air, and want of exercise, above all among schoolgirls kept indoors. The book is an early work on stress, plain in advice and humane in tone, though its views on women are dated.
13234-ester-ried:
Pansy's Ester Ried, published in Boston by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard and illustrated by Elizabeth Withington, follows a young woman's moral growth. Chapters run from Ester's home and what Sadie thought to Florence Vane, the Sunday lesson, and a journey to cousin Abbie. Pansy, author of Julia Ried and The King's Daughter, writes for girls and young women.

At dinner, Ester raises a wineglass to her lips, guided by her own conscience, not her uncle's, while Abbie's glass stays untouched and color mounts on her face. Later, a house holds both wedding finery and funeral crape, as life and death touch close. Ester's story is a Sunday-school novel of conscience, family, and faith, plain in style and earnest in aim.
13522-superseded:
May Sinclair's 1906 novel Superseded, republished in America at her wish as her best work before The Divine Fire, first appeared with another work as Two Sides of a Question. Miss Quincey stops the way in the prologue, household gods, inaugural addresses, and Dr. Bastian Cautley follow, with healers, regenerators, spring fashions, and a painful misunderstanding.

Rhoda speaks to Miss Cursiter, and next day her secretary grants Miss Quincey three months' leave, her place kept. Miss Quincey, now a person of importance, finds old Martha unnaturally attentive and Mrs. Moon conceding her right to be ill. Through a stethoscope, bills, and an epilogue on the man and the woman, Sinclair writes of a woman superseded, then quietly reasserting herself.
13652-exposition-of-the-apostles-creed:
The Rev. James Dodds expounds the Apostles' Creed article by article, opening with Luther's table talk: an old doctor of divinity who has not got beyond children's learning. The Ten Commandments, the Belief, and the Lord's Prayer, studied daily with his son John and daughter Magdalen.

Dodds divides each article into sections, from I believe in God the Father Almighty, maker of heaven and earth. Through Jesus Christ his only Son our Lord, conceived by the Holy Ghost and born of the Virgin Mary, to suffering, death, and resurrection. To call Christ our Lord, he argues, is to renounce other masters and claim victory and salvation. The book is a plain, pastoral guide to the creed for ordinary believers.
1401-tarzan-the-untamed:
Edgar Rice Burroughs sets this Tarzan tale in Africa during the First World War, when German troops raid Tarzan's home and scatter his household. Tarzan answers with a lone campaign of vengeance, moving through jungle, lion country, and enemy lines in search of those who wronged him.

Along the way he finds an aeroplane, a black flier, and at last the walled city of Xuja, where a mad queen rules a people shut off from the world. The chapters pile up fights, escapes, and strange rites. It is a fast, violent jungle adventure built on loyalty, revenge, and Tarzan's code of the wild.
14444-the-complete-english-tradesman-183:
Daniel Defoe's manual, first issued in 1726 and reprinted in Edinburgh in 1839, instructs a young man on how to run a shop and stay solvent. Defoe, himself a trader turned writer, speaks from hard experience.

Chapters cover apprenticeship, letter writing, diligence, overtrading, credit, bankruptcy, and the ruin brought by extravagant living or early marriage. He warns against leaving business to servants and against trusting debtors too far. The book is blunt, practical, and full of anecdote, a classic guide to eighteenth-century commerce. Its blunt advice on credit and debt still sounds familiar to modern shopkeepers today.
14498-a-handbook-to-the-works-of-brownin:
Mrs. Sutherland Orr's handbook to Robert Browning, first written for the Browning Society in 1885 and reaching a sixth edition in 1892, guides readers through the poet's long and difficult works. This reprint carries the same text.

Orr summarizes poems in order, explains speakers and plots, and follows Balaustion from her first adventure through Aristophanes' Apology, after Euripides' death and Athens' fall. Her notes untangle Browning's dense allusions without flattening them. The handbook served generations of Browning readers, and it still helps newcomers find their way into his dramatic monologues. Orr knew Browning personally, which lends her notes quiet authority.
14644-the-development-of-the-european-na:
J. Holland Rose, fellow of Christ's College, Cambridge, wrote The Development of the European Nations, 1870 to 1914, reaching a fifth edition in 1915 with a new preface and three supplementary chapters. Rose also wrote lives of Napoleon and William Pitt.

Chapters move from the causes of the Franco-German War through Worth, Gravelotte, and Sedan. They continue to the founding of the French Republic and the German Empire, then to the Eastern Question and the Russo-Turkish War. Rose argues that Turkey's misfortunes owed much to its own customs and creed. The book is a solid, old-fashioned survey of Europe's road to war.
14723-how-it-happened:
Kate Langley Bosher's How It Happened, illustrated and published in September 1914, is a light domestic romance by the author of Mary Cary and The Man in Lonely Land. Bosher dedicates it to her friend Ariadne Elizabeth Vaughan Latham.

The heroine begins by smashing a high-crowned, narrow-brimmed hat of stiff gray felt, her Christmas present to herself, after holding it at arm's length. Later she weighs a solemn supper question: sardines with lemon, or toasted cheese on toast with syrup afterward? A visit from Miss Barbour and her father's plans round out a gentle, cheerful novel.
15074-his-majesties-declaration-defended:
John Dryden's 1681 pamphlet defends King Charles II's Declaration touching the recent dissolution of Parliament, answering a seditious letter from a person of quality. Godfrey Davies supplies a modern introduction in this Augustan Reprint Society edition, published at Los Angeles in 1950. The pamphlet takes the form of a letter to a friend.

Dryden argues, in sharp Restoration prose, that the king acted within his rights and that his critics stir faction. The piece shows the poet as a political polemicist, not just a playwright. Students of Stuart politics and of Dryden's prose will find it a compact, fierce sample of pamphlet war.
15127-pitman-s-commercial-spanish-gramma:
C. A. Toledano's 1917 commercial Spanish grammar teaches the language for trade, not just for school. It opens with the full alphabet, from a to z with ñ, ll, and rr, and notes that k and w appear only in foreign words. Vowel sounds follow, each matched to an English example, with stress rules added.

Later lessons build business vocabulary, verb forms, and letter writing for merchants and clerks. The approach is practical: speak, read, and write Spanish well enough to do business. Students of old language manuals will find the book clear, systematic, and firmly rooted in the commerce of its day.
15191-the-commercial-products-of-the-veg:
P. L. Simmonds's huge 1854 handbook treats plant products used by man, from tropical trees to garden crops, for colonists, makers, merchants, and buyers. It covers growing, preparing for shipment, and market value, with notes on arts and manufactures. Subscribers from steamship firms to farm societies front the book.

Entries range across fibers, dyes, oils, gums, spices, and timbers, each with practical detail on use and trade. Simmonds, a longtime editor of colonial magazines, writes for workers, not scholars. The handbook remains a rich source on Victorian trade in plant goods and on empire's material life.
15696-superstition-unveiled:
Charles Southwell, author of Supernaturalism Exploded and Impossibility of Atheism Demonstrated, published this freethought tract in London in 1854, with Edward Truelove of the Strand. Southwell abridged it from his Apology for Atheism, and opens with a warning: know your gods before you worship them. The book argues that religion shapes every relation and condition of life.

Southwell insists the link between religious faith and political practice is far closer than generally thought. Religious error, he writes, is the intangible but real substratum of all political injustice. A people in superstition's fetters cannot secure political freedom, he argues, even when reformers admit Islam's influence on Constantinople yet act as if Christianity had little to do with England's politics. The tract is a Victorian atheist's case against priestcraft and for free thought.
1602-dawn-o-hara-the-girl-who-laughed:
Edna Ferber's Dawn O'Hara follows a girl who laughed through a smash-up, mostly eggs, and a move to a new life steeped in German, coffee, and coffee cake. Dawn develops a homesickness, meets Blackie and his philosophy, and faces a lady from Vienna and a tragedy of gowns, all with humour and pluck.

Ferber, writing early in her career, gives Dawn a reporter's eye and a comic voice, and the novel moves from American towns to European rooms. The dedication teases her mother and sister for interruptions and shushing. Dawn O'Hara is a bright, early Ferber novel of a girl making her way.
16441-the-closet-of-sir-kenelm-digby-kni:
Anne Macdonell edited this 1910 edition of Sir Kenelm Digby's famous seventeenth-century receipt book, with introduction, notes, and glossary. Receipts for mead, metheglin, and other drinks open the collection, followed by a long run of cookery receipts, a table of dishes, and notes on the powder of sympathy. A list of herbs and flowers closes the useful matter.

Digby's closet gives a lord's kitchen and stillroom in full: wines, meats, sweets, and cures side by side. Macdonell's notes help modern readers follow old measures and terms. Food historians will find it a feast, both as history and as a source of dishes still worth trying.
16611-anson-s-voyage-round-the-world-the:
H. W. Household cut down the classic tale of Commodore Anson's round-the-world voyage for school use, with his own lead-in, notes, and word list. Rivingtons put the short text out in London in 1901. It follows the squadron from its aim and ships, through Madeira, storms, scurvy, Juan Fernandez, wrecks, and fights at sea.

The short form keeps the hard facts: bad weather, sick crews, lost consorts, and the wreck of the Wager with its mutiny. Notes and a word list help a young reader track old sea terms and places. The book gives a brisk, true sea story of risk and endurance, trimmed to fit a class book without losing its drive.
17047-the-half-hearted:
John Buchan's novel, set in the closing years of the 1800s, opens in Glenavelin, a green hill land of fir woods, meadows, and sea breezes. Part One follows a gentleman among country guests, gardens, and conferences of power, until pride, conscience, and a Rubicon crossing push him toward a hard choice. Part Two takes the road east, to hill forts, outposts, and a chief's tactics.

The tale mixes Scottish pastoral with imperial adventure, and its hero's half heart gives the book its name. Buchan writes with a brisk, outdoor vigor, and the hills stay vivid throughout. Readers who like early Buchan will find a thoughtful adventure about courage found late, and duty faced at last.
17198-the-botanical-magazine-vol-01-or-f:
William Curtis's Botanical Magazine, volume one from 1790, shows foreign plants grown in open ground, greenhouses, and stoves, drawn in their true colors. Each plant gets its name, class, order, and character after Linnaeus, plus its home, its flowering time, and the best way to grow it. The work aimed at ladies, gentlemen, and gardeners who wished to know their plants in a scientific way.

Curtis, author of Flora Londinensis, sold the magazine from his botanic garden at Lambeth Marsh. Its preface tells how subscribers begged for such a guide to garden plants. Plant lovers and garden historians will enjoy this first volume, where fine plates meet plain, useful culture notes.
1724-finished:
Near the end of his career, Allan Quatermain meets a new cast — Anscombe, Marnham, Doctor Rodd, and Heda, a young woman driven toward a marriage she hates. A game of cards, a flight, and a hunter hunted carry the plot through country where debts and guns settle most arguments.

Quatermain, near the end of his career, acts as protector and witness, and the book reads as a farewell to the character Haggard had written for decades. Readers who have followed Allan from King Solomon's Mines will find the tone graver here. The adventures shadowed by the knowledge that this hunter's road is running out.
17435-the-days-of-mohammed:
Anna May Wilson wrote this life of Mohammed, published in 1897 by the David C. Cook Publishing Company of Elgin, Illinois, and Chicago. The book tells the days of Mohammed, from his early life through his mission and the founding of a new faith, in the plain style of a popular religious biography. Cook, a publisher of Sunday school and family books, issued it for general readers.

Readers get a late nineteenth-century American telling of the Prophet's story, respectful in tone and simple in form. The book suits readers interested in how Mohammed's life was presented to English-speaking households of its day. Its interest today lies as much in its period voice as in its subject.
17531-the-botanical-magazine-vol-02-or-f:
William Curtis, author of Flora Londinensis, issued this second volume of the Botanical Magazine, or Flower-Garden Displayed, printed in London by Couchman and Fry for Curtis. The magazine shows the most ornamental foreign plants grown in the open ground, the greenhouse, and the stove, accurately represented in their natural colours. Its motto, from Verulam, calls a garden the purest of human pleasures.

Each plant entry adds names, class, order, and generic and specific characters after Linnaeus, with places of growth and times of flowering. Readers get the founding work of illustrated botanical publishing, beautiful and systematic at once. The volume suits gardeners, botanists, and lovers of botanical art.
17672-the-botanical-magazine-vol-03-or-f:
The third volume of William Curtis's Botanical Magazine, or Flower-Garden Displayed, continues the founding work of illustrated botanical publishing. Like its companions, it shows the most ornamental foreign plants grown in the open ground, the greenhouse, and the stove, accurately represented in their natural colours. Each entry adds names, class, order, and characters after Linnaeus.

Places of growth, times of flowering, and the most approved methods of culture complete each account. Readers get Curtis's magazine at full stride, beautiful and systematic at once. The volume suits gardeners, botanists, and lovers of botanical art, as a companion to the second volume.
17979-the-botanical-magazine-vol-04-or-f:
William Curtis wrote the Botanical Magazine, or Flower-Garden Displayed, and this fourth volume was printed in London in 1791. Curtis, author of Flora Londinensis, aimed his work at ladies, gentlemen, and gardeners who wished to know the plants they grew.

Each entry shows a choice foreign plant in its true colors, with its name, class, order, and marks after Linnaeus. It also gives its home, its bloom time, and the best way to grow it. The volume opens with annual lavatera. It is a lovely, learned garden book, and a fine relic of the age when botany was both science and polite art.
18107-american-lutheranism-vindicated:
S. S. Schmucker wrote American Lutheranism Vindicated in Baltimore in 1856, printed by T. Newton Kurtz. Schmucker, professor of theology at Gettysburg, examines the Lutheran symbols on disputed topics, with a reply to the Reverend W. J. Mann's plea.

Chapters run from the Augsburg Confession and the authority of creeds to the Definite Platform, the Diet of Augsburg, and Melanchthon's alarms. Schmucker holds creeds subordinate to Scripture, and human creeds fallible. The book is a learned, period work of American Lutheran debate, best for students of church history, doctrine, and the old fights over creeds.
18654-what-might-have-been-expected:
Frank R. Stockton published this novel at New York in 1874. It opens in Virginia, where children Harry and Kate Loudon worry over old Aunt Matilda, a beloved neighbor who cooks for them and tells queer old stories. News that she must go to the almshouse sets Harry on a bold plan. The tale follows his adoption scheme, business ventures, and a grand scheme for a line of some sort.

Later chapters bring a turkey hunter, a lively team, a council, board meetings, business telegrams, and profits and projects, with Kate anxious throughout. Stockton mixes humor, pluck, and country life in his easy style. The novel is a warm example of his fiction for young readers.
1889-bird-neighbors-an-introductory-acqu:
Neltje Blanchan introduces readers to one hundred and fifty birds of the eastern United States in Bird Neighbors, a friendly guide for beginners. Each bird gets habits, song, nest, and field marks in plain language. Blanchan, writing as Neltje Blanchan, helped found the Audubon movement's popular side.

Blanchan writes for people who watch birds near home, not for ornithologists alone, and her book helped start popular bird study in America. The guide remains charming, though later books give more exact science. Her one hundred and fifty birds, described by song and habit, invite beginners outdoors.
18964-wolf-breed:
Jackson Gregory published this western novel in 1916, with a color frontispiece by Frank Tenney Johnson. The story opens at open house at Père Marquette's, where a girl stands on a bearskin rug scattered with a thousand minted gold pieces. Around her gather figures with names like No-Luck Drennen and the man under the cloak.

From that glittering opening, the novel follows fortune, luck, and loyalty in northern ranch and mining country. Promises, idols, and a girl sent to live among wolves, in the chapter titles' phrase, drive the plot. Readers get a romantic western built on gold, danger, and proud characters, in Gregory's popular magazine style.
19087-the-king-nobody-wanted:
Norman F. Langford wrote this 1948 life of Jesus for young readers, with pictures by John Lear. Chapters move from waiting and birth to growing, work, friends and foes, refusal of a crown, the road to Jerusalem, and the last night and day. The style is simple and direct throughout.

Joseph tells shepherds how he and Mary came to Bethlehem for the census, found no room at the inn, and slept in a stable where the baby was born. The shepherds, first to hear the angels' song, carry the news at dawn. Young readers get a clear, gentle retelling of the Gospel story.
19123-the-botanical-magazine-vol-05-or-f:
William Curtis wrote this fifth volume of The Botanical Magazine, a work on ornamental foreign plants grown in open ground, glass houses, and hot houses. Each plant is shown in natural colours, with its Linnaean class, order, and character, plus its place of growth and time of flowering. Gardeners, ladies, and gentlemen were its intended readers.

Entries give approved methods of culture beside the plates, from orchids brought from Jamaica to spring bulbs like Bulbocodium. One orchid flowered at Chelsea after roots were nursed in rotten wood and leaf mould. Readers get a handsome, useful garden reference from the age of plant collecting.
19472-branded:
Francis Lynde wrote this western novel, put out in New York in the late nineteen teens with a frontispiece by Arthur E. Becher. Its chapters run from the heating of the iron and the searing touch to scars, a downward path, and a good Samaritan, all signs of a man marked by law and shame.

A blasting scene in a gulch, with rock and dust bursting from a shallow hole, shows Lynde's taste for workaday danger. The novel follows its hero westward toward a cup of trembling and a plain-clothes man, asking whether a branded man can win a clean name.
19933-cluthe-s-advice-to-the-ruptured:
Cluthe's Advice to the Ruptured is a medical advertising booklet about hernia. It compares rupture unfavorably with poor eyesight. Glasses that improve sight are easy enough to get, it says. Only a small share of rupture sufferers ever find real support. Most find nothing that even keeps the rupture from growing worse. The Cluthe truss is then offered as that rare support. Charles Cluthe's firm sold trusses from New Jersey for decades.

Before safe hernia surgery, trusses were the standard answer. Makers competed with booklets of advice and testimony. Cluthe's mixes anatomy, warning, and salesmanship in that order. Such ephemera document everyday medicine before hospitals dominated. The booklet survives as honest period quack-adjacent print. It shows sufferers addressed as customers first.
20330-the-black-wolf-s-breed:
The Black Wolf's Breed, from 1899, is a historical tale set under Louis XIV. Its people are king and courtier, soldier and diplomat, lass and lady. Brave fighting and loose swords fill the stage, the preface warns. Honor clings to an empty shadow in that glittering, faithless court.

The women seem more fair than honest, the writer adds with a shrug. He begs readers to recall when these things happened, and where. France under the Sun King gives the tale its pomp and peril. Readers get swashbuckling romance in a court of spies and swordsmen.
20866-infantry-drill-regulations-united-:
Distance, in drill terms, means the space from one man's back to the next man's breast. The 1911 Infantry Drill Regulations fix that gap at forty inches in line and column. Each term in the book gets that same crisp, fixed sense.

These rules governed how American infantry marched, formed, and fought in 1911. Officers drilled companies by its words on fields across the country. The corrected text shows an army on the edge of modern war. Students of military history can trace in it the last full bloom of close-order drill before machine guns rewrote the field.
21351-the-prayer-book-explained:
Percival Jackson of Jesus College, Cambridge, published the first part of The Prayer Book Explained in 1901. It covers the daily offices and the litany of the Church of England. He quotes Hooker at the start: the book requires but orderly reading. His preface defends the service book against easy distrust.

Jackson argues that the spirit of worship rests on faith in God, in the words used, and in the people worshipping together. He explains each office's structure and history for churchgoers who say the words weekly without knowing their roots. A second part was to follow on the rest of the Prayer Book.
21498-france-and-the-republic-a-record-o:
William Henry Hurlbert toured the French provinces in 1889 and wrote France and the Republic. The year was the centennial of the French Revolution, and the republic marked it in state. Hurlbert, who had written on Ireland under coercion, brought a sharp eye to France.

He weighs French republican rule against Swiss and American practice, and finds it wanting. Chapters treat Gambetta's rise, the powers of the executive, and the reach of the legislature. A map backs his record of things seen and learned on the road. The book is a frank, hostile tour of a young republic at one hundred years.
21738-hunted-and-harried:
Dragoons cross the river Cairn in Dumfriesshire on a bright morning in this Ballantyne tale of seventeenth-century Scotland. The troop rides for the moors near Skeoch Hill, mud-spattered from a long hunt. Their young officer rides ahead, and one trooper's face carries a sadness the others lack. They are hunting men, not game.

The story belongs to the years when Scotland's Covenanters were chased across their own hills for their faith. Ballantyne tells it from both sides of the hunt, soldier and fugitive. Faith, mercy, and cruelty meet on the moors in his telling. It is one of his most serious books, built on a dark and well-remembered page of Scottish history.
21843-the-botanical-magazine-vol-06-or-f:
Foreign flowers in their true colors fill this sixth volume of William Curtis's Botanical Magazine, the famous flower-garden journal. Each plant is drawn and colored from life, then described by name, class, and order in the system of Linnaeus. Curtis adds where each plant grows, when it flowers, and the best way to grow it. The work served ladies, gentlemen, and gardeners who wanted science with their pleasure.

Curtis had won fame with his Flora Londinensis before starting the magazine. Volume by volume, the series became the most loved botanical periodical in English. Gardeners still prize its plates for accuracy and beauty together. This volume keeps the standard: exact botany, plain culture advice, and flowers shown as they truly look.
21873-planet-of-the-damned:
Brion steps into a temple of hooded, empty-eyed men in Harry Harrison's Planet of the Damned. The story first ran in Analog magazine in 1961, then became a Bantam book in 1962. Something evil infects the planet, and the still figure at the room's center moves with crazy menace. Brion knows at once that he has found the enemy. The tale builds from that chill into full science fiction adventure.

Harrison, also author of the Deathworld books, writes fast and lean. His hero must grasp a whole world's madness before he can fight it. The book became a staple of paperback science fiction shelves. It shows Harrison's gift: a strange world, a hard problem, and a man thinking his way through both at speed.
21892-at-the-time-appointed:
A lonely mountain station under a fierce noonday sun opens A. Maynard Barbour's At the Time Appointed, first published in 1903. The line winds far above the level of the sea. A stranger dismounts there to meet a woman who comes swiftly toward him, hand extended. Barbour had won her readers with That Mainwaring Affair, praised in its day for thrills worthy of Anna Katharine Green.

Reviewers quoted on this edition stress the plot's adroit turns and the clean, excellent style. The story works as mystery without cheap sensation, they said. Darrell, the man of the frontispiece, carries the tale through the mountain West. Twelve editions by this printing show how well it pleased. It is a polished popular novel of love and hidden wrongs.
22152-possessed:
Cleveland Moffett, a journalist who wrote Through the Wall, published the novel Possessed in 1920. He swore the story rested largely on fact. It opens at a party in a Washington Square apartment in New York. Soft lights, low divans, and a painted ukulele set a scene of fashionable ease at Bobby Vallis's gathering.

There a sudden, dramatic prophecy is spoken over the company. The rest of the book follows that prophecy toward its strange fulfilment. Moffett mixes society comedy with the occult interests of the post-war years. Possessed belongs to the brief craze for psychic fiction that followed the Great War's losses.
22240-masterpieces-of-negro-eloquence-th:
Masterpieces of Negro Eloquence, published in 1914, gathers the best speeches delivered by Black men and women in America. Alice Moore Dunbar edited the volume, then writing as Alice Dunbar. Its speeches plead, accuse, and argue across a century of struggle. One early oration calls on Christian philanthropy to reconcile the races and points to Africa as the field for its work.

Frederick Douglass, Booker T. Washington, and many lesser-known orators stand in its pages. Church, congress, and convention platform all contribute. Dunbar meant the book as proof of a people's genius with words. It remains a handy one-volume record of African American public speech before the Harlem Renaissance.
22403-poems-of-gerard-manley-hopkins-now:
Poems of Gerard Manley Hopkins were first published long after his death. Robert Bridges, his friend, edited them with notes. Bridges kept the poems for years before letting them appear.

His verses to Hopkins call that legacy coy in his home. Hopkins's heart, he writes, once sought shelter under God's terror. Beauty and sorrow held the young poet aghast in life's wild wood. His rare talent went in disdain, ill-brokered and unpraised. Yet love of Christ, Bridges hoped, would win man's love at last. The poems that follow changed English poetry. Their springy rhythms and dense images struck readers as startlingly new.
22973-the-english-husbandman-the-first-p:
Gervase Markham offers his idle hours' work to noble readers in The English Husbandman. Its first part contains the knowledge of husbandry, the rules and maxims of farming fitted perfectly, he assures us, to the English climate. How well or ill the book is done, he writes, his lordship's wisdom must judge and correct.

Beneath the courtesy stands a practical manual of the early seventeenth century. Plowing, sowing, livestock, and seasons fill its chapters in the spelling of the day. Markham wrote for gentlemen farmers who ran real estates with real tenants. Few books show everyday Tudor and Stuart farming so closely. Readers willing to slow down for old type will find a working farm between these covers.
23198-with-no-strings-attached:
With No Strings Attached is a naval science-fiction story set aboard a United States submarine. Other boats named for Washington, Patrick Henry, and Benjamin Franklin can circle the globe without surfacing for air. For a vessel meant to run on diesel and electric power, such a feat should be rare.

A few crew members have seen what goes on in the battery room. They are, of all the crew, the most secretive and the most puzzled. That split drives the tale: most sailors serve a boat they half understand, while a small few guard a secret about how it truly runs.
23388-wrecked-but-not-ruined:
R. M. Ballantyne set this Canadian tale at a fur traders' outpost on the northern shores of the Gulf of Saint Lawrence, a cluster of low wooden houses tucked under a rugged cliff. Around them lies vast, empty country, reached by a rude road that winds through snow and cold wind.

The traders, hardy pioneers of the fur trade, face wreck, want, and the long northern winter, yet hold together through work and faith. Ballantyne knew this country well, and he fills the tale with its sights, its seasons, and its lonely grandeur. Readers who love the Canadian north will find a stirring story of ruin met with grit, and of a small outpost that refuses to give up.
23579-the-botanical-magazine-vol-07-or-f:
William Curtis, author of Flora Londinensis, wrote this seventh volume of the Botanical Magazine, or Flower Garden Displayed, for ladies, gentlemen, and gardeners who wished to know plants by science. Ornamental foreign plants, grown in open ground, greenhouse, and stove, are shown in their natural colours.

Each plant gets its name, class, order, and characters after Linnaeus, its place of growth and flowering time, and the most approved methods of culture. Opening verse ranges far and wide through gardens' pride, where jasmines deck walls, woodbines breathe fragrance away, and myrtles form shade. Gardeners and flower lovers will value the volume as a beautiful, practical guide to growing exotics well, in an age when a greenhouse was a mark of taste.
23611-why-they-married:
James Montgomery Flagg wrote and drew this nineteen hundred six book of why they married, printed by Life Publishing Company and dedicated to several obliging married couples who posed for portraits. An opening verse begs readers not to be ashamed to say why they tried matrimony, for others brave the undertow for reasons quite as funny.

Portraits follow in verse and picture. A gentle chap stung by wedding a forceful Miss Howe wins everyone's sympathy. Maud hung onto subway straps where no man offered a seat and swore she would marry the first man who did. More couples follow in turn. Flagg draws with wit and a light, satiric touch, poking at love, pride, and convenience. Readers who like comic verse will enjoy the book as a bright, Edwardian joke book on marriage.
23845-talents-incorporated:
Murray Leinster published Talents, Incorporated in 1962, a science fiction novel about unusual human gifts put to work. Its hero is young Captain Bors, who planned and carried out the destruction of a warship because information about its existence and location was verified, as he believed, by a magnetometer.

Bors is shaken to learn how that information was really obtained. It was guessed at by a discharged spaceport employee, a paranoid personality, and a man who used a hazel twig or something similar. Had he known, he would have dismissed it flatly. Leinster's story turns on talents that look like science, feel like guesswork, and carry deadly consequences when trusted.
23958-the-romance-of-words-4th-ed:
Ernest Weekley's The Romance of Words, in a fourth edition, studies the origin and life of English words with the scholarly method his reviewers praised. The Spectator commended his handling of a subject left mostly to the amateur or the crank, and Truth found surnames under his guidance full of fascination.

Weekley, who also wrote The Romance of Names, Surnames, and an Etymological Dictionary of Modern English, shows how words travel, change, and keep their histories. New words of his day, from copec and fascist to insulin and rodeo, enter his dictionaries for the first time. For readers who love language, the book makes etymology a romance in its own right, without unnecessary dullness.
23996-jewel-weed:
Alice Ames Winter, author of The Prize to the Hardy, published Jewel Weed in New York in 1906, with illustrations by Harrison Fisher and a dedication to her parents. Its twenty-two chapters move from a light from the far East to another beginning.

Mother and son, an Occidental luminary, and days at Madeline's lead to salad days and the chapter Jewel Weed itself. Lena's progress, the falls, an invitation, and bitter-sweet give way to politics and play, an engagement, and an awakening. The return of Ram Juna, a honeymoon, Lena's friends, and grape-shot precede Easter and Oriental rubies. A light from the East goes out, a light in the West goes down, and the novel begins again.
24015-a-masque-of-days-from-the-last-ess:
Walter Crane newly dressed and decorated A Masque of Days from the Last Essays of Elia, published by Cassell in London, Paris, New York, and Melbourne in 1901. Elia is Charles Lamb, and Crane's full-page illustrations carry each paragraph of Lamb's fancy.

With the old year dead and the new year of age, the young spark gives a dinner to which all the days in the year are invited. The festivals, deputed as stewards, have long provided mirth for mortals below and now want a taste of their own bounty. Whether the fasts should be admitted is stiffly debated, but Christmas Day, with a design upon Ash Wednesday, overrules the objection. Only the vigils, with lanterns, are asked to light the gentlefolk home.
24119-make-mine-homogenized:
Rick Raphael wrote this comic science fiction tale for Astounding Science Fiction in April 1960, with pictures by Freas. It is set on a Nevada ranch. Hetty Thompson starts her hot morning by counting eggs in the henhouse and scolding her rooster Solomon for strutting while five eggs come up short. The ranch yard, the hens, and the heat set a plain farm scene.

Into that scene comes the tale's tall premise, flagged on its first page as the world's most potent eggnog. Raphael plays the joke straight, letting farm sense meet wild science for laughs. Readers get a short, sunny spoof in which a ranch woman faces a fizzy bit of inventive trouble.
24188-the-strand-magazine-vol-05-issue-3:
This number of The Strand, an illustrated monthly, is volume five, issue thirty, dated June 1893. It opens with Pierre and Baptiste, by Beckles Willson, about two hard-working mechanics at Sault aux Beloeuil, each with a wife and half a dozen children to support. They labor far into the night, and their pillow, the tale insists, is hard earned, though how they earn it depends largely on the police.

One November evening the pair plans the burglary of a safe in a wholesale house in St. Mark Street, where the head book-keeper wrestles with accounts that will not balance. An error of several hundred dollars has run through each day's footing. Readers get a lively magazine mix of crime, humor, and pictures, in the Strand's popular style.
24340-the-common-sense-of-socialism-a-se:
John Spargo, author of The Bitter Cry of the Children and Socialism: A Summary and Interpretation of Socialist Principles, wrote this book of letters to Jonathan Edwards of Pittsburg. Charles H. Kerr and Company published it in Chicago in 1911, with copyright in 1909. It is dedicated to George H. Strobell, as a token of friendship and love. Spargo opens by noting that socialism is undoubtedly spreading, and therefore deserves a plain hearing.

Chapters ask what is the matter with America, and describe the two classes in the nation. They show how wealth is produced and distributed, and name the drones and the bees. They trace the root of the evil from competition to monopoly, state what socialism is and is not, answer objections, and ask what shall we do, then. Readers get a direct, letter-form case for socialism, in plain American prose.
24469-the-supplies-for-the-confederate-a:
Major Caleb Huse wrote this brief memoir of his four years as purchasing agent in Europe for the Confederate States during the Civil War. Friends who heard his stories at his Hudson home, The Rocks, in the summer of 1903 urged him to write them down, so that a unique piece of history would be preserved.

Huse describes buying arms, ships, and supplies abroad, and the tangled business of paying for them and shipping them past the Union blockade. His account is short, but no one else could have given it. Readers interested in the Civil War's hidden side, its finance and foreign supply, will find here a firsthand record of great value.
24580-ship-bored:
Julian Street wrote this humorous book, published with illustrations by May Wilson Preston. Its title puns on being bored aboard ship: a long ocean voyage, with its spotters, deck games, and fellow passengers, can try even a cheerful traveller. One caption jokes about a charming spotter, and a wife's twelve lost dresses.

Street, author of Paris a la Carte and My Enemy the Motor, writes light, observant prose about travel manners and shipboard life. His sketches poke fun at tourists, stewards, and himself. Readers who enjoy gentle travel humour will find this short book a pleasant companion for a voyage of their own.
24670-the-botanical-magazine-vol-08-or-f:
William Curtis edited this eighth volume of The Botanical Magazine, or Flower-Garden Displayed. In it, the most ornamental foreign plants, grown in the open ground, the greenhouse, and the stove, are shown in their natural colours. Each plant entry gives its name, class, order, and generic and specific characters after Linnaeus.

Entries also give places of growth, times of flowering, and the most approved methods of culture. Curtis aimed his work at ladies, gentlemen, and gardeners who wished to know their plants scientifically. The volume remains a beautiful record of Georgian gardening, prized by plant lovers and collectors of botanical art.
2501-a-face-illumined:
E. P. Roe's Face Illumined follows a young woman whose plain face and inner light draw the love of those who learn to see her truly. The novel's romance turns on character rather than beauty, with Roe's earnest, ministerial voice guiding the story toward faith and affection. The heroine's growth gives the book its arc.

Roe's popular fiction aimed at the heart, and this novel shows his method at its warmest. Modern readers will find its sentiment old-fashioned but sincere. It offers a window into the best-selling fiction of its day.
25171-the-uncalled:
Paul Laurence Dunbar's Uncalled, copyrighted in 1898, is a novel of small-town life in Ohio. It opens on a cold winter morning in Dexter, where snow has half melted into mud and the houses stand black and dripping in the meanest part of town.

Neighbors watch and talk, and much of the story moves through back-fence gossip between women such as Mrs. Martin and Mrs. Smith. Dunbar, famous for his Lyrics of Lowly Life, writes here in prose about ordinary people, their judgments, and the quiet pressures of church and community.
25185-mysteries-of-bee-keeping-explained:
M. Quinby's Mysteries of Bee-Keeping Explained, published in New York in 1853, sums up more than twenty years of work in extensive apiaries. Quinby, a practical bee-keeper, promises the natural history of bees and directions for gaining the most pure surplus honey at the least expense.

Chapters describe queens, workers, and drones, weigh rival hives, and warn against patent-hive speculators. Readers learn feeding methods, remedies for losses, and the plain craft behind what Quinby calls the science of luck. The book remains a clear window on American beekeeping before modern hives.
25607-witness-to-the-deed:
George Manville Fenn writes this novel, in which an admiral's young daughter had wed a forger, thought dead. The hero, due that day to marry her and very much in love, is stopped on his way to church by a visitor with news.

Fenn uses flashbacks in early chapters, unusual in nineteenth-century fiction, which can puzzle readers at first but reward patience. The tale turns on a deed witnessed, a past marriage, and a forger's return, mixing domestic feeling with mystery in a style few but Fenn could sustain.
25637-the-dark-house-a-knot-unravelled:
George Manville Fenn writes this short murder and detection mystery, praised by its transcriber as masterly, full of suspense and surprises, and unusual for a nineteenth-century book. The story opens after a rich recluse dies, his strange will pointing to a fortune concealed in his home.

Most people at the reading never knew the dead man in person, yet received kindnesses such as school and university fees. The principal beneficiary, a great nephew, also never knew him. Only the old lawyer who dealt with him really knew him, and unravelling the knot means tracing kindness, greed, and secrets through a dark house.
25682-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
H. J. L. J. Masse, author of books on Tewkesbury Abbey and Deerhurst Priory, describes the cathedral church of Gloucester in this Bell's Cathedrals guide, with forty-nine pictures. The first edition came in January 1899, a second in August 1900, and a reprint in January 1905. Gloucester Cathedral from St. John's Church roof fronts the book.

Masse gives a description of the fabric and a brief history of the episcopal see. The series aims to supply visitors with accurate, well pictured guides at a popular price, scholarly enough for students of archaeology and history yet plain enough for ordinary visitors.
25706-federal-bureau-of-investigation-fo:
This file gathers Federal Bureau of Investigation documents released under freedom of information law. Transcriber notes say censored words appear as underscores. Handwritten comments and stamps are noted at each document's end. Disc and disk spellings vary in the originals and are kept.

An urgent teletype from Portland on 11 August 1947 opens the run, reporting flying discs as a security matter. A former navy pilot, now near Myrtle Creek, Oregon, reported seeing a mysterious object twice. He saw it on the evening of 6 August while flying at about five thousand feet. Hatfield was to be interviewed, and Washington recorded and indexed the message in October 1947.
26199-fables-of-john-gay-somewhat-altere:
John Benson Rose printed this 1871 volume for private circulation, presenting it with affection to his niece Margaret Rose. His dedication recalls her childhood, when she spoke no English at one visit and no French at the next, and how she begged him for a big book all her own. He answers with a thin book instead, and with brevity as his rule.

The volume reworks John Gay's fables in shorter, altered form, and it compresses Chaucer's Flower and Leaf into little. Later fables include a florist who pets a pig, then begs it to spare his tulips. The book mixes family warmth with old moral tales, retold in plain verse for a young reader's shelf.
26330-frenzied-finance-vol-1-the-crime-o:
Thomas W. Lawson's Frenzied Finance, volume one, subtitled The Crime of Amalgamated, appeared in New York in 1905, reprinted from Everybody's Magazine. Lawson of Boston dedicates the book to penitence and punishment, hoping exposed wrongdoers repent and unpunished crimes win public disgrace. A portrait shows Lawson after twelve months of the series.

The volume chronicles high finance as a chain of graft within the law, with lawyers, lieutenants, and water carriers serving a master named Whitney. Margin calls force stocks overboard, sinking prices and dragging friends' holdings down like falling bricks. Lawson calls his targets average men met on life's bridge, not monsters. The book stands as a classic muckraking attack on stock-market power.
26713-norman-ten-hundred:
A. Stanley Blicq published this battalion record with the Guernsey Press Company in 1920, subtitled a battalion from the oldest and smallest democracy in the world. It records the First Service Battalion, Royal Guernsey Light Infantry, the Norman Ten Hundred given by the States of Guernsey for active service beside the mother country's troops. Blicq calls the narrative authentic.

Guernsey, Sarnia to the Romans, sent Norman warriors to Duke William at Hastings in 1066 and kept the independence granted for their valour. Some seven thousand Guernsey men went out into the Great Undertaking. Chapters run from September and October 1917 through the Cambrai rehearsal and offensive. They continue through Marcoing and Masnieres and the German onslaught of late November. The Passchendaele sector leads to Doulieu and Estaires in April 1918. Men arrive fed up after thirty-six hours in cattle trucks, hearing distant guns.
26754-one-thousand-secrets-of-wise-and-r:
C. A. Bogardus, champion quickshot of the world, published this household and oratorical miscellany at Springfield, Missouri, copyrighted in 1898 and revised and enlarged as a fourteenth de luxe edition in 1907. Bogardus explains that former editions were well liked except for small type, so the new edition appears in larger type.

His preface borrows Agesilaus of Sparta, who said boys should learn what they will practice as men, and divides man's duties into household economy and national economy. Departments cover quick shooting records, medicine, accidents and poisons, ink, cosmetics, live stock, hogs, poultry, chemicals, and miscellany, including inventions, candy-making, rare coins, and memory systems. Speeches by Patrick Henry, Lincoln, and Bryan close a book promising a thousand secrets of wise and rich men.
26875-the-boy-scout-fire-fighters-or-jac:
Major Robert Maitland wrote this fourth volume of the Boy Scout Series, published by the Saalfield Publishing Company in 1912. Seventeen chapters open with the Thirty-ninth Troop in camp on a Saturday afternoon, hard at signal practice, semaphore, and Morse flag signaling. A pall of dark, threatening smoke hangs over a wooded mountain, and a circular ring in the blackness proclaims a spreading fire.

Jack Danby, head office-boy where he and Tenderfoot Pete Stubbs both work, is sent with Pete toward the fire by Scout-Master Thomas Durland. They must learn whether bare ground will resist the flames or stubble and short dry growth will feed them, and whether any small brooks lie hidden. Later chapters bring a spy, an attack on the station, Jack's peril, a burning launch, and the dynamiters.
27118-mother-earth-vol-1-no-2-april-1906:
Mother Earth, volume one, number two, for April 1906, is Emma Goldman's monthly magazine of social science and literature, ten cents a copy from 210 East 13th Street, New York. The contents open with John Davidson's poem To the Generation Knocking at the Door, urging readers to break tradition open.

Emma Goldman writes on The Child and Its Enemies, L. I. Peretz on Hope and Fear, and John R. Coryell on Marriage and the Home. A visit to Sing Sing, Max Baginski on the old and new drama, and notes on the modern newspaper fill a number that argues for freedom in every department of life.
27181-prof-koch-s-method-to-cure-tubercu:
Dr. Max Birnbaum's Prof. Koch's Method to Cure Tuberculosis, translated from the German by Dr. Fr. Brendecke and published at Milwaukee in 1891, explains Robert Koch's claimed cure in popular form. The translator's preface calls consumption curable and tuberculosis the most terrible of foes, creeping into the system before its presence is surmised.

Koch, once a poor and obscure student, is hailed as a deliverer, and the book adds his first communication from the Deutsche Medizinische Wochenschrift with explanatory notes. The volume captures the excitement, and the hope, that greeted Koch's announcement.
27222-the-tin-box-and-what-it-contained:
Horatio Alger Jr.'s The Tin Box and What It Contained follows Harry through a collision, signs of a tempest, and losing his place after all. Mrs. Ross makes two unsatisfactory visits, Uncle Obed arrives from Illinois with a proposal, and a notice to quit sharpens the plot.

Philip meets his match, two conspirators scheme, and Harry's trips to the wood bring a commission, a reward offered, and the finding of the box. Chase is brought to justice, Philip is forced to apologize, and Harry becomes a bondholder, in Alger's cheerful tale of pluck rewarded.
27457-the-woman-who-dared:
Epes Sargent published this work with Roberts Brothers in Boston in 1870, entered for copyright in 1869, under a motto from John Milton, pitting honest liberty against dishonest license. That motto points to the theme of a woman who dares to claim liberty against license.

Sargent's dedication, itself in verse, tells how his rhythmic structure grew day by day at Strawberry Hill. The lawn sloped green to the trees, the Hudson's tide rolling beautifully on, with purple gleams on the Palisades. The poem that follows keeps that blend of domestic peace, taste, and beauty with a firm moral stand. It is a graceful example of post-Civil War American verse.
27680-uncle-sam-s-boys-in-the-ranks-or-t:
H. Irving Hancock's 1910 boys' novel opens his Uncle Sam's Boys series, following two recruits into the United States Army. The story begins with arguments about soldiering at home and moves through the recruiting office, medical examination, and awkward-squad drill.

Later chapters take the young soldiers to Fort Clowdry, guard duty, a mail-train detail, and a mystery at post three, with hazing, pranks, and danger along the way. Hancock wrote to stir respect for the uniform while giving readers a detailed picture of army routine. Hancock was already known for his West Point and Annapolis series when he wrote for boys who admired army life.
28064-the-relations-of-the-federal-gover:
Joseph K. Edgerton delivered this speech at Fort Wayne, Indiana, on October 30, 1860, on the eve of the Civil War. Its subject is the relation of the federal government to slavery, and its hero is Stephen A. Douglas, whom Edgerton defends against partisan attack. The speech was printed as a vindication of Douglas's stand for the Union and the Constitution.

Edgerton argues that the Constitution rested on mutual concession, and that Douglas sought to hold North and South together under it. He recalls Douglas's final efforts to unite northern Democrats behind the government. The text gives a direct view of Democratic argument in the canvass of 1860.
28179-the-inglises-or-how-the-way-opened:
Margaret Murray Robertson's The Inglises, published in 1872, is a novel of a Canadian township and a minister's family. Reverend Mr. Inglis preaches in Gourlay Centre, Gourlay Corner, and the North Gore, while his household faces illness, loss of income, and the hard choices of women left without support. Robertson writes of religion-minded folk with care.

Sickness in that age often meant death or a long bed, and a breadwinner's death could leave a family bare. Faith, neighbours, and plain duty carry the Inglises through. The novel gives modern readers a clear picture of nineteenth-century home life, before doctors and social reform changed it.
28484-the-philosophy-of-the-conditioned:
H. L. Mansel was a professor of moral thought at Oxford, and in 1866 he published The Philosophy of the Conditioned. The book reprints essays from the Contemporary Review, with additions, and it defends Sir William Hamilton against J. S. Mill and Herbert Spencer.

Mansel holds that Hamilton's main rule is to take mind as a whole. The absolute, he says, cannot be grasped by bare reason, yet faith in a personal God still stands on moral feeling. Spencer keeps only the negative half of Hamilton, and Mansel shows why that half alone will not do. The book is a clear Victorian debate about knowledge, faith, and God.
2854-sir-francis-drake-revived:
Philip Nichols, preacher to Francis Drake's company, wrote this account of Drake's voyages to the Spanish Main, later reviewed by Drake himself. The text was prepared from a 1910 edition and draws on reports by men who sailed with Drake, including Christopher Ceely and Ellis Hixom. It follows the building of storehouses, the help of escaped enslaved Africans called Cimaroons, and raids planned across scattered islands.

The narrative gives a contemporary English view of Elizabethan seafaring, with supply, shelter, and surprise mattering as much as battle. Drake appears as a careful planner rather than a mere raider. The book still serves as a primary account of how England's most famous sea captain actually organized a voyage.
28575-a-terminal-market-system-new-york-:
Mrs. Elmer Black's A Terminal Market System, copyrighted in 1912, calls New York's markets its most urgent need. The city, with over five million people, has no effective market system: buildings stand out of repair, organization is slight, and administration lost eighty thousand dollars to the treasury in a year. Population nearly quadrupled in a generation while markets stayed as they were.

Boston, Baltimore, New Orleans, Buffalo, and Cleveland all profit from municipal markets, Black notes, with figures to prove it. A tour of Europe follows, from Covent Garden, Smithfield, and Billingsgate to Berlin, Munich, and the Paris Halles. Readers get a reformer's brief, built on comparison.
2876-the-light-that-failed:
Rudyard Kipling's novel The Light That Failed follows Dick Heldar, a war artist whose sight begins to fail as his career rises. The dedication verses to his mother promise a love that would follow him to hill, sea, or damnation. The story tests that promise through London studios, friendships, and a romance with Maisie. A seaside visit to Fort Keeling finds the pair sitting under a cannon, remembering an old breakwater.

Blindness becomes the novel's center, forcing Dick to face what his art and his pride are worth when he can no longer paint. Kipling writes the studio world with sharp detail and the love story with unusual tenderness. The book endures as a portrait of an artist losing the very sense his work depends on.
28803-the-works-of-mark-twain-an-index-o:
David Widger edited this index to the Project Gutenberg editions of Mark Twain's works. Rather than a single novel, it gathers the contents of Twain's books in one place. Its pages list Huckleberry Finn, Tom Sawyer, Life on the Mississippi, The Innocents Abroad, A Connecticut Yankee, and Pudd'nhead Wilson, beside many sketches, speeches, and stories. Both illustrated and unillustrated editions are listed, with volumes of his letters.

The index serves as a map for readers who want to find a particular Twain title or chapter among the many Gutenberg files. It names the works, groups them by edition, and notes where the autobiography stands on copyright in different countries. Anyone exploring Twain's long career can use it to plan a reading path through his novels, travel books, and short pieces.
28850-the-project-gutenberg-works-of-joh:
Edited by David Widger, this linked index gathers the Project Gutenberg editions of John Lothrop Motley's histories. Motley lived from 1814 to 1877 and wrote The Rise of the Dutch Republic, The History of the United Netherlands, and The Life and Death of John of Barneveld. The index lists every volume and chapter, from Philip the Second in the Netherlands through the administration of Alva. A memoir of Motley by Oliver Wendell Holmes appears as well.

The volume is a finding aid for a great nineteenth-century historian of the Netherlands' fight for freedom from Spain. Its chapter lists let a reader follow Motley's long narrative year by year, from 1555 to 1623, without hunting through separate files. Anyone studying the Dutch revolt or Victorian historical writing can use it to plan a path through Motley's shelf.
28879-a-popular-history-of-france-from-t:
David Widger edited this linked index to Francois Pierre Guillaume Guizot's Popular History of France, translated by Robert Black and illustrated by A. De Neuville. The index covers six volumes, from antiquity to 1100 through 1715 to 1789, with chapter lists for each. The first volume runs from Gaul and the Gauls out of Gaul through Roman conquest, the Franks and Clovis, Charlemagne, and feudal France to Hugh Capet.

Guizot, a great French historian and statesman, wrote for general readers, and his history pairs narrative with over four hundred engravings and woodcuts. The index lets a reader find any period, from Vercingetorix's surrender to Caesar to the Crusades, without hunting through separate files. It serves as a guide to one of the classic popular histories of France in English.
29139-no-pets-allowed:
M. A. Cummings wrote this short science fiction story about a future state where pets of any kind are forbidden. The narrator, sent far out to work alone for four months, found company in a creature he cannot tell anyone about, since believers would punish him for having her. The tale opens with a council scene. The chief of vocation reports he has tried the young man on a dozen jobs, and his intelligence seems no greater than that of twentieth-century ancestors.

The council agrees no idle person can exist in the state, and one old member proposes making him guard of the treasure. Cummings, praised for her earlier story The Weirdies, writes a hauntingly persuasive tomorrow that may not gleam as hoped. Readers get a quiet, strange tale of loneliness, rules, and a forbidden friendship.
29227-the-politician-out-witted:
Samuel Low wrote this comedy in five acts, printed for the author in 1789 and extracted here from Representative Plays by American Dramatists, volume one. Low, born December 12, 1765, remains little known: the editor found almost nothing about him except his birth date and his anti-federalist sympathies. The play was chosen as representative of early American drama reflecting the political spirit of its time.

Characters include Old Loveyet and Tabitha Cantwell, and the plot turns on a politician outwitted by sharper players. Low's comedy reads well beside Dunlap's work of the same years. Readers get a rare early American political comedy, partisan and lively, from the first year of the federal government.
29315-australia-revenged:
The writer calling himself Boomerang published this novel in London and Sydney in 1894 with Remington and Company. Boomerang's preface says each character is a type. The Australian characters, he says, may be met every day in the colonies. Villiers Wyckliffe and the Detlij Club are not distorted figments of imagination. The broken heart, he adds, symbolizes the aims of one party and the object of the other.

Chapters run from the Detlij Club through confidences, the mia-mia, the ball, the oath, and revenge, then through Adelaide, Melbourne, cabbies, Launceston, Goodchild's, Port Arthur, Hobart, and Sydney. Colonial governors appear in a less heroic light than usual, with an appendix to explain the standpoint. Readers get a colonial Australian novel of society, revenge, and politics, sharp about its world.
29350-the-ancient-monuments-of-north-and:
C. S. Rafinesque published this second edition, corrected, enlarged, and with additions, on the ancient monuments of North and South America. Rafinesque was professor of historical and natural sciences. He belonged to many learned societies, from Philadelphia and New York to Paris, Bordeaux, and Copenhagen. He writes of massive ruins and the arts and skill they show.

The book surveys mounds, earthworks, and stone remains across the Americas, arguing for their antiquity and importance at a time when American archaeology was young. Rafinesque's claims were often speculative, and modern readers should treat them as period science. Readers get a pioneering, if uneven, survey of American antiquity, valuable for its enthusiasm and its early attempt to map a continent's monuments.
29384-disowned:
Victor Endersby's short tale, printed in Astounding Stories in September 1932, opens in a summer storm that changes one man's life for good. A narrator sheltering with his brother Tristan and Tristan's fiancee under a great oak feels a strange pull toward the sky. The storm, the tree, and the dread of height set up a misadventure in which the sky itself turns into an appalling abyss.

Endersby follows the man as the pull grows, drawing him ever upward and cutting him off from home, kin, and solid ground. The tale blends dread, fate, and a touch of the weird with plain, tense prose. Fans of early pulp tales of strange science will find a short, haunting story about fear made real.
29503-the-hated:
Paul Flehr's short tale opens in a nameless bar across the river from New York, in a town the narrator thinks is Hoboken but cannot swear to. The bar's sign reads only Cafe, Eat, Cocktails, which makes little sense, but it has a big television blaring in three colors and a jukebox trying to drown it. The narrator likes the place, though his contract says he should stay in New York and New England.

Flehr's tag line promises that beyond space, one more river waits: the far shore of hate and murder. The tale follows a man who gets a girl someplace, usually not much, and finds trouble waiting. Fans of hard, pulp science fiction will enjoy a moody, street-level story of hate and flight.
29678-the-epistles-of-st-peter-and-st-ju:
Martin Luther preached and explained the epistles of St. Peter and St. Jude at Wittemberg in 1523 and 1524, in this translation by E. H. Gillett, printed in New York in 1859 by Anson D. F. Randolph. Gillett found the works among dusty piles of old pamphlets high on the shelves of the Union Theological Seminary library, in original editions issued during Luther's lifetime.

Gillett's preface notes that Luther's commentary on Galatians, fine as it is, runs too long and costs too much for wide circulation, while these shorter expositions travel better. The book gives Luther's plain, forceful reading of two short, stern epistles. Students of Reformation thought will find a valuable, early English rendering of Luther the preacher.
30251-disqualified:
Charles L. Fontenay sets a short inspection tale on an alien world, with pictures by Kelly Freas, in which an overlord must qualify for Solar Council aid. After a morning inspection tour, Tardo, the council's Planetary Aid agent, and his companion Peo are taken to a castle on a hill. Saranta, wealthy overlord of that portion of the planet, entertains them royally at luncheon. Tender inch-thick steaks in delicate wine sauce, exotic vegetables, and cool fruit dessert fill the meal.
