Tardo warns that his recommendation matters greatly: a favorable word brings technical aid from the ship at once, while advanced equipment waits on a fuller investigation. Saranta modestly doubts that a simple, agrarian culture can win approval, and Tardo lists fundamental requirements, from no abnormal religious practices to no slavery. The tagline hints the test: the most secretive things are often the most obvious.
30419-how-to-form-a-library-2nd-ed:
H. B. Wheatley, F.S.A., writes How to Form a Library, second edition, in The Book-Lover's Library edited by Henry B. Wheatley, published in New York by A. C. Armstrong and Son and in London by Elliot Stock in 1886. Wheatley notes in his preface that a guide to the formation of libraries is allowed to be required. Doing so large a subject justice is hard, and that difficulty kept would-be authors from attempting it.

He hopes it will not count as temerity that he stepped into the vacant place. He doubts he has done justice to so important a theme, given the brief space available, yet believes the volume holds much information. The librarian and the book lover require it and cannot easily obtain it elsewhere. Memory fails at times, he adds, and then a record at hand is convenient.
30429-was-man-created:
Henry A. Mott, Jr., PhD, asks Was Man Created? A New York volume from Griswold and Company, 150 Nassau Street, in 1880, carries it, with an illustration of the fossil man of Mentone from Popular Science Monthly, October 1874. Mott, member of the American Chemical Society, the Berlin Chemical Society, and the New York Academy of Sciences, also belongs to the American Association for the Advancement of Science. He belongs to the American Pharmaceutical Association, and to the Geographical Society, and writes as author of the Chemists' Manual.

His other works include Adulteration of Milk and Artificial Butter. The work was written to be delivered as a lecture. As its pages multiplied, friends urged him to publish it as a book, and at last Mott agreed. It does not claim a discussion of the departments it treats, but presents the observations in each department in as plain a form.
30443-the-strand-magazine-vol-05-issue-2:
This May 1893 issue of The Strand Magazine presents an illustrated monthly mix of fiction for a general reader. It is volume five, number twenty-nine. Its opening story is In the Shadow of the Sierras by Iza Duffus Hardy. Barbara Thorne sorts a dusty drawer of old letters, papers, and account books when a photograph stops her work.

Lost in memory, she stares at the image and the past it recalls. That quiet domestic opening is typical of the magazine's illustrated tales. The issue format pairs such stories with pictures, giving Victorian readers short, complete fiction in a handsome monthly package. As a periodical number, it captures the Strand's blend of sentiment, mystery, and everyday life.
30468-holes-incorporated:
L. Major Reynolds writes Holes Incorporated, a science fiction tale that warns what happens when a person makes holes in nothing at all, pushes steel beams through them, and heads for the hills. Ted Baker and Bill Stephens arrive for a three-thirty appointment with H. Joshua Blair, booked two weeks earlier.

A red-headed secretary checks them off her list and asks their business. Ted holds out a small steel box and says it is for construction work, because it makes holes. The secretary, late in the day, cares little at first. Reynolds builds a comic yet alarming premise around a device that could let all hell break loose.
30872-a-collection-of-state-papers-relat:
Printed in London in 1782, this collection of state papers marks the first acknowledgment of the sovereignty of the United States by the States General of the Netherlands. It also records the reception of their minister plenipotentiary. It opens with a political character of John Adams, ambassador from the states of North America, written by an American, and it also carries Adams's essay on canon and feudal law. The book sold for two shillings.

Its core is Adams's memorial to their High Mightinesses, the States General of the United Provinces, proposing a treaty of amity and commerce with full powers from Congress. For readers of the American Revolution, the papers show diplomacy at work: a new republic seeking recognition, trade, and standing among European powers. It is a short, formal, and historically weighty set of documents.
31100-the-complete-project-gutenberg-wor:
Edited by David Widger, this single volume gathers eight works by Jane Austen. They are Persuasion, Northanger Abbey, Mansfield Park, Emma, Lady Susan, her early writings collected as Love and Freindship, Pride and Prejudice, and Sense and Sensibility. The set opens with Persuasion, dated 1818 in the text, where Sir Walter Elliot of Kellynch Hall pores over his book of baronets.

Across the novels, Austen studies courtship, money, family pride, and the gap between sense and show, usually through a sharp-eyed heroine learning to judge character. Having the whole run together lets a reader trace her range from youthful satire to mature comedy. The volume serves as a handy one-stop shelf for her complete fictional work.
31200-the-wide-awake-girls-in-winsted:
Katharine Ruth Ellis's 1909 girls' book, published by Little, Brown in Boston with drawings by Sears Gallagher, follows Catherine Smith of Three Gables and her Wide Awake Girls. Part one, Starting a Library, opens with Catherine's inspiration, a song for her alma mater that proves harder to write than her full heart expects. It then moves through getting started, organization, and work with pail and broom.

Later chapters bring an opening, a party at Polly's, Brookmeadow, arrival at Winsted, Sunday school, journalism, the three R's, and a last party, ending with auf Wiedersehen. Dedicated to Gladys Goddard, friend of many boys and girls, the book is a warm story of girls' enterprise, friendship, and good work.
31302-the-negro-what-is-his-ethnological:
Published in Cincinnati in 1867 under the pen name Ariel, this second edition asks what the Negro's ethnological status is. Is he the progeny of Ham, a descendant of Adam and Eve, possessed of a soul, or a beast in God's nomenclature? What status did God fix for him in creation, and what is his relation to the white race?

The author insists the slavery question is not involved and not discussed, and that the points are purely ethnological and Biblical. He argues both common assumptions are false. The Negro descends neither from Ham, youngest son of Noah, nor from Adam and Eve, and he claims the Bible, concurrent history, and facts outside the Bible settle the matter. The book is a document of nineteenth-century polygenist argument, valuable as evidence of how racial science was argued from scripture.
31341-apparitions-or-the-mystery-of-ghos:
Apparitions, or the Mystery of Ghosts, Hobgoblins, and Haunted Houses, Developed, gathers stories of hauntings and strange sights, with an illustration of the Haunted Beach dated 1814. A Monthly Review notice quoted in the book, from October 1814, praised the collection as well chosen and cheap at five shillings. It argued that putting such a book into children's hands would guard their minds against weak credulity more effectually than grave philosophic admonition.

The collection's purpose is therefore double: to entertain with ghost stories and to teach readers, especially the young, to doubt them. Tales of haunted houses and hobgoblins sit beside an implied lesson in clear thinking. For modern readers, the book is both a period ghost anthology and a document of early efforts to answer superstition with reason.
31392-the-inhabited:
Richard Wilson's story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in January 1953, sends a sexless creature naked through the dimension stratum as first traveler to Earth. It is a sort of spy and fifth-columnist on a mission from which return is uncertain. Its job is to learn whether Earth suits habitation by its fellow beings, whose own world is about ended and who must move or die.

The creature's first stop, unfortunately for its dignity and equilibrium, is inside the mind of a cat, chosen as a lower animal whose mind should be easy to control. The magazine's illustration frames the joke: containing a foe is sound military thinking, unless carried out so literally that everybody becomes an innocent Trojan horse. Clever and strange, the tale turns invasion into a comedy of embodiment.
31507-peggy-raymond-s-vacation-or-friend:
Harriet Lummis Smith's Peggy Raymond's Vacation, or Friendly Terrace Transplanted, continues the Peggy Raymond series. Its earlier volumes include Peggy Raymond's Success, or The Girls of Friendly Terrace, and Peggy Raymond's School Days. The vacation volume opens with "The Exodus" in mid-June, when Peggy, silent for three-quarters of an hour unless asked a question, gives answers that do not fit. Later chapters promise a rescue and a home sweet home.

The story transplants the Friendly Terrace girls to a summer setting, where old friendships meet new scenes. Smith, also author of Pollyanna books, writes for girls with warmth and humor. The novel's appeal is its circle of friends, carried intact into vacation, and the small adventures that test them away from home.
31825-portia-or-by-passions-rocked:
Portia, or By Passions Rocked, by the Duchess, author of Phyllis and Airy, Fairy Lillian, opens with a carriage rolling down a long dark avenue beneath tall elms and copper beeches. Through them, the dying sun flings its parting rays. The horses, sniffing the air of home, quicken until they draw up before the hall door.

On the stone steps stands a very pretty girl, eager and expectant. She runs down to greet a visitor two years older than herself, a girl whose tone is slow and sweet, almost to languor. Readers get a Victorian society romance of passion, friendship, and country houses, in the popular manner of its fashionable author.
31970-feline-red:
Robert Sampson's short story Feline Red was printed in Planet Stories in January 1954. It opens in riot in an engine room, where Chief Engineer Durval shouts orders from the bridge above the hulking atomics. A scattering of compact, darting, poppy-colored beasts scuttles into an engine's shadow, while heavy wrenches club futilely behind them.

Its sidenote warns that it is up to Jerill to think fast, before those strange beasts suck away the last purified ore on the freighter Bertha. First Mate Scott Jerill, grim and lean-faced, orders the men back: there is no time to drive the cats out like this. Readers get a brisk space tale of cats, ore, and a quick-thinking mate.
32205-the-woodlands-orchids-described-an:
Frederick Boyle's The Woodlands Orchids was published in London and New York by Macmillan in 1901, with coloured plates by J. L. Macfarlane. It describes orchids and tells stories of orchid collecting. Boyle, author of Camp Notes and About Orchids, A Chat, republished tales of orchid-seeking by licence. The licensing papers were the Pall Mall Gazette, the Sunday Times, Black and White, Chambers's Journal, Wide Wide World, and Badminton Magazine.

Boyle writes that the work needs no preface, but hopes his tales will amuse the general reader, while other portions prove useful to orchid growers. Plain descriptions of rare species and varieties, he notes, are hard to find elsewhere. Readers get two books in one: adventure stories from orchid hunting, and a grower's guide to rare orchids, illustrated in colour.
32320-the-art-of-illustration-2nd-ed:
Henry Blackburn's handbook, in a second edition published in London in 1896, explains modern systems of book and newspaper illustration. Blackburn, editor of Academy Notes and Cantor lecturer on illustration, wrote for artists facing a swift change in the trade. With ninety-five illustrations, the book shows how drawing for process printing was replacing wood engraving.

Line drawing gets the fullest treatment, since illustrators now had to turn tone into line for reproduction. Blackburn covers pen work, photo-zinc and other processes, and the practical needs of daily and book work. The volume suits students, teachers, and working artists who want a clear, period guide to how pictures reached print in the 1890s.
32395-no-strings-attached:
Lester del Rey's tale, printed in IF Worlds of Science Fiction in June 1954, centres on Henry Aimsworth, an unhappy husband who cannot bear the sight or sound of his wife, Emma. Divorce is not open to him, since Emma likes being his wife, and Henry has brooded over the problem of a perfect murder. The story opens by weighing how a stranger's killing might leave no motive, clue, or suspect.

Henry's case is harder, since husbands always rank high among suspects. Help arrives in the form of Alféar, a genie who, like most people, is a creature of habit. Together they form a murder compact meant to leave no strings attached. Del Rey plays the bargain for dark humour, as each neat plan creates a new tangle for its makers.
32430-the-practical-joke-or-the-christma:
The Practical Joke, or The Christmas Story of Uncle Ned, published in New York by J. S. Redfield, opens with a warm welcome to Christmas and New Year, prized by children above all other days. Christmas Eve brings stockings, Santa Claus, sugar-plums, a cheerful fireside, merry games, and happy faces, while the eldest sister shares her mother's councils and helps distribute presents. On Christmas morning, lazy and industrious children alike rise bright and early to inspect stockings.

After supper, when youngsters are warned of bedtime, a loud call rises for a story from Uncle Ned. In trim leg, home-knit stocking, bright shoe-buckles, drab small-clothes, and a queer continental hat, Ned takes his silver-mounted cane and begins. His tale recalls his boyhood, when, a slip of a lad full of fun, he nearly lost his own life and a friend's at a pond.
32614-the-diary-of-a-resurrectionist-181:
James Blake Bailey prints a resurrectionist's diary for 1811 and 1812, with an account of the resurrection men in London and a short history of the Anatomy Act. Students then needed proof of two courses of dissection, yet lawful bodies were scarce, so grave robbers supplied the schools.

Bailey first traces that grim trade, from watched graves to houses where bodies were kept until useless. The diary itself then logs night after night of work at Bunhill Row, Bethnal Green, and St. Thomas's, naming hauls and buyers in blunt, businesslike entries. The book is grim, but its tone stays factual. It shows how law, need, and crime shaped early medical training.
32659-an-answer-to-a-scurrilous-pamphlet:
This London pamphlet of 1693 answers Monsieur de Cros and defends Sir William Temple's Memoirs. Its writer says friends urged him to reply, though Temple's fame had little to fear from so feeble an attacker. He calls de Cros a rambling scribbler whose letter promises more than it performs.

Point by point, the answer justifies passages de Cros attacked, from talks at Nimeguen and the Hague to the secrets of King Charles's court. It also drops hints of intrigues not well known before. The pamphlet is a sharp piece of Restoration polemic, where wit serves as a weapon in a quarrel over history.
32711-disaster-revisited:
Darius John Granger tells of Jason Wall, a very rich man of about forty-five. His doctor tells him he has eighteen months, perhaps two years, to live. There is no chance of a cure. Wall rages at the unfairness, since he can buy anything except health.

Outside his window the world goes on playing, indifferent to his death. He answers with a crash program to build a time machine. Within ten months the machine is complete. Its physicists assure him that actions at the level of molecules and atoms are reversible. Wall must decide whether revenge is worth erasing everyone.
32722-jewish-theology-systematically-and:
K. Kohler, president of Hebrew Union College, sets out Jewish theology in a systematic work published by Macmillan in 1918. Fifty-nine chapters fall into three parts: God, Man, and Israel with the Kingdom of God. The book moves from the meaning of theology and the essence of Judaism to faith, law, and hope.

Chapters weigh revelation, prophecy, and Torah, then God's unity, power, mercy, and justice. Later parts treat free will, sin, repentance, prayer, and death, and close with election, the messianic hope, and the synagogue. Kohler writes for readers who seek both reason and reverence in Jewish faith.
32745-the-unlearned:
Raymond F. Jones tells of Dr. Sherman Hockley, Chief Officer of Scientific Services, Information and Coordination, in this story from IF Worlds of Science Fiction of August 1954, illustrated by Ed Emsh. Hockley administers Earth's information files and the National Laboratories, choosing which projects get money when Congress allots enough for one or two.

Then come rumors from Rykeman III, whose scientists are conceded supreme in scientific achievement. The Rykes will answer any question Earth is intelligent enough to ask, for a price. Thar urges Hockley to follow them. Hockley hesitates, stubbornly wanting to weigh the answers against their costs, and to take one short step on Earth's own two feet.
33128-a-collection-of-gospel-hymns-in-oj:
Printed for the International Evangelical and Colportage Mission of Algoma and the North-West, the second edition from Sarnia in 1899 gives hymns in two languages for Canada's north-west. Depots stood in Toronto and Rochester, New York. The book's first hymn, in long meter, opens with all people that on earth do dwell. It sings to the Lord with cheerful voice, in the familiar words of the old psalm paraphrase.

The collection's purpose was practical: to let Ojibway-speaking congregations sing the gospel in their own tongue, with English beside it for teachers and visitors. As a document it preserves Ojibway language in print at a time when mission presses were among its main publishers. For students of hymnody, translation, and northern missions, it is a small, valuable source.
3316-how-members-of-congress-are-bribed:
Joseph H Moore addresses this open letter, protest, and petition from a citizen of California to the United States Congress. Its subject is the lobbyist, and Moore defines the creature unsparingly. He is a persistent intermeddler without proper warrant in government affairs, an unscrupulous dealer in threats and promises among public men, and a constant menace to sworn servants in offices of trust.

The lobbyist, Moore adds, tempts the corrupt and terrifies the timid who serve the people. The pamphlet names the machinery of bribery as its author saw it: pressure, money, and fear applied where laws are made. It survives as a Progressive-era protest, blunt and specific, from a citizen who believed Congress itself should hear the charge in plain words.
33274-the-abbatial-crosier-or-bonaik-and:
Eugene Sue's tale, part of his Mysteries of the People series on a proletarian family across the ages, centers on Bonaik and Septimine in a medieval world of monks, slaves, and power. The abbatial crosier, a bishop's staff, stands at the heart of a story about church rule, bondage, and the fate of common folk. Sue sets his people against great forces, letting their lives show how history pressed on the poor.

The novel belongs to a long series that follows one family from age to age, each volume taking a new era and a new emblem. Here the medieval church and its lands frame a tale of love, faith, and resistance. Readers who enjoy sweeping historical fiction with a social edge will find a vivid, earnest chapter in Sue's vast family saga.
33512-hard-pressed:
Fred M. White opens this sporting mystery on a gala night at London's National Opera House, where a fashionable audience gathers to hear Melba in a new part. Among them sit a girl and two men whose fortunes will soon tangle with rogues, temptations, and racing trials on the Downs. The forty-two chapters move from opera boxes and clubs to empty houses, eavesdroppers, and a soldier of fortune.

Confessions, an ultimatum, a poisonous atmosphere, and a dramatic exit raise the stakes as the hero is pressed from two sides at once. White balances racing detail with detective suspense, and the closing chapters bring the chase to the racecourse itself. Readers who enjoy Edwardian thrillers of sport and villainy will find a fast, eventful plot here.
33516-abandoned:
Jules Verne, translated by W. H. G. Kingston, continues a castaway adventure in this Everyman's Library volume. The party, including Cyrus Harding, Neb, Herbert, Pencroft, and Gideon Spilett, builds a canoe, hunts, climbs a great kauri tree, and explores an island that shows no sign of human presence. A wreck on the coast yields a case of tools, weapons, instruments, books, and utensils that changes their prospects.

Later chapters follow journeys along rivers and coasts, encounters with monkeys and waterfalls, and the slow work of mapping and surviving. Verne's pleasure lies in practical ingenuity: how castaways turn wreckage and island resources into shelter, food, and transport. Young readers and fans of Robinsonade adventure will enjoy its blend of exploration and problem-solving.
33564-john-bull-junior-or-french-as-she-:
Max O'Rell, author of John Bull and His Island, turns his Gallic wit on translation itself in this 1888 volume, with a preface by George C. Eggleston. The subtitle, French as she is traduced, puns on translation and slander. Pirate publishers and their translators, Eggleston complains, not only carried O'Rell to American readers. They also improved his books by adding flashes of their own invention, things never found in the French originals.

O'Rell's subject is the Englishman abroad and the Frenchman as seen by English eyes, with American humor as a third ingredient. The book jokes about national character, language, and manners, while its preface jokes about literary piracy. Readers who enjoy nineteenth-century comic travel writing will find a lively, if period-bound, satire of how nations misunderstand one another in print.
33716-manners-and-rules-of-good-society-:
A member of the aristocracy sets out the manners and rules of good society, or solecisms to be avoided, in this thirty-eighth edition, published in London and New York in 1916. The contents run from introductory remarks and the meaning of etiquette through introductions, leaving cards, paying calls, precedency, the colloquial use of titles, etiquette toward royal personages, traveling abroad.

Further chapters cover dinner giving and dining out, dinner-table etiquette, evening parties, weddings and their expenses, and afternoon at homes. They also cover colonial and Indian etiquette, garden parties, luncheons, breakfasts, picnics, and juvenile parties. The book is a complete guide to Edwardian social correctness, and a rich source for historians of manners.
33725-unexplored:
Allen Chaffee writes a boys' adventure of the outdoors in this 1922 book, illustrated by William Van Dresser. Twelve chapters follow Ted Smith from a rodeo and a camping trip through living off the wilderness, work with the air patrol, a daring feat, incendiaries, a cave, a snow-slide. A glossary and pronouncing dictionary of geological terms, with a key to geologic time, closes the volume.

Chaffee, also known for Lost River and the Twinkly Eyes books, mixes camping skills, geology, and frontier excitement. Ted's adventures teach as they entertain, turning a fossil find into a lesson in deep time. Young readers who enjoy nature, camping, and exploration will find a sturdy, old-fashioned adventure with a real scientific thread.
33735-pamela-censured:
Pamela Censured, first published in 1741, is a contemporary attack on Samuel Richardson's immensely popular novel Pamela, or Virtue Rewarded. It was reprinted by the Augustan Reprint Society in 1976 with an introduction by Charles Batten Jr. The pamphlet belongs to the storm of praise and parody that greeted Richardson's story of a servant girl whose virtue is rewarded. It argues against the novel's morals, plausibility, and literary merit.

Notes to the introduction cite letters from Aaron Hill to Richardson in December 1740 and from Knightley Chetwood in January 1741, together with the Gentleman's Magazine. They place the pamphlet in the first months of Pamela fever. For students of the early novel, the reprint offers a sharp, period voice of dissent, showing that Richardson's triumph was contested from the very start.
34052-wireless-transmission-of-photograp:
Marcus J. Martin wrote this manual on sending photographs by wireless, in a second edition revised and enlarged in 1919, published in London by the Wireless Press. A preface to the second edition opens the book, and figures, including figure ten, aid the text. Martin explains how a picture can be broken into signals, sent through the air, and rebuilt at the far end.

The manual serves engineers, operators, and students of early radio, with working detail on apparatus and method. It shows a new art at the moment when wireless pictures first seemed practical. The book remains a clear record of an early step toward fax and television.
361-miss-billy-married:
Eleanor Porter picks up Billy's life just after her wedding to the artist Bertram in this sequel. The book opens at the altar, then follows the young couple as they set up house, face money cares, and learn the hard art of married talk. Friends, kin, and a small child soon add their own claims on Billy's time.

Quarrels, dinners gone wrong, and well-meant meddling test the pair, yet Porter keeps the tone kind and comic. Billy learns to manage a home without losing her brisk self. The novel closes as a warm, light study of early married life, full of talk, tact, and second thoughts.
3674-the-dragon-and-the-raven-or-the-day:
George Alfred Henty writes a boys' adventure novel set in the days of King Alfred, when Danes invaded England. His preface notes that school histories pass briefly over Alfred's reign, and that the incident of the burned cake is what most readers remember. The chapters follow fugitives, the battle of Kesteven, the massacre at Croyland, the invasion of Wessex, a disciplined band, and a Saxon fort.

The hero sails in a ship called the Dragon, cruises against the Norsemen, endures a siege of Paris, and reaches the Isle of Athelney, Alfred's refuge. Henty mixes battle, seamanship, and loyalty to king and faith. The book suits young readers who enjoy historical adventure and the making of England.
3830-overruled:
Bernard Shaw pairs a provocative preface with a one act play in this volume. The preface, called The Alleviations of Monogamy, insists the piece is no argument for or against polygamy, but a clinical study of how such tangles occur among quite ordinary people. Shaw notes that theoretic libertines usually live blameless family lives, while practical libertines preach severity to everyone else.

The play tests the point, as Gregory courts Mrs Juno under a cloud of misunderstanding about her late husband. She calls him poor Tops, and Gregory takes the endearment for a widow's grief, only to learn that Tops is very much alive. Shaw's comedy turns on that shock, and on how quickly respectability bends when feeling enters.
39445-hoyle-s-games-modernized:
Hoyle's Games Modernized is a book of games edited by Professor Hoffmann. This new edition was reset and fully revised to 1909. Fresh chapters on auction bridge and three other new games came from Ernest Bergholt, as the title page states. New chapters on other games stand in the book as well, as the head breaks off.

A note by the transcriber states the shape of the text. A few slips of print have been set right, and they are listed at the end of the book. The first page numbers are shown in the text as figures in curly brackets. The ebook was made ready by Orphaned Projects and the Online Distributed Proofreading Team. A picture form of the book stands in the Gutenberg stock as well. The work is a modern rule book in the old Hoyle line, brought up to its day.
4305-the-unclassed:
George Gissing wrote this early novel about people who fit no neat class: neither quite poor nor quite respectable. The contents run from school and mother and child through Christmas in two homes, an advertisement, and the cousins, to rent day, a man-trap, and the Enderbys. Later chapters promise art and misery, straying, and freedom.

The story follows young men and women trying to rise by learning, work, and love, while London keeps pulling them back. Gissing's sympathy is with strivers whose manners outrun their means. The Unclassed shows the novelist finding his subject: the borderland between classes in late Victorian England.
4311-the-emancipated:
George Gissing wrote this novel of emancipation in two parts, set partly in Italy and partly in England. The first part follows northerners in sunlight, Cecily Doran, a boarding-house on the Mergellina at Naples, and a martyr's story. Later chapters bring the dead city, an appeal to authority, and a declaration.

The second part returns to England, with the proprieties defended, deniers in England, a stay at Paestum, and Cecily's return. Gissing's theme is freedom from old faiths and old rules, and what that freedom costs. The novel suits readers who like Gissing's serious treatment of belief, art, and the new woman.
4392-martie-the-unconquered:
Kathleen Norris wrote this novel, volume eight of her collected works, around Martie and her California village life. It opens on a windy, warm September afternoon, as four girls leave the post office at Monroe, California. They have wasted time on an unnecessary errand, and now they saunter into the street, disheartened by the slow afternoon.

At five they plan to sit at Bonestell's drug store soda counter, drinking fruit syrups and soda waters. From that small-town opening Norris builds a long story of a woman who refuses to be conquered by circumstance. The novel is domestic fiction at large scale, following Martie through youth, marriage, and the trials of a full life.
4532-tom-swift-and-his-photo-telephone-o:
Victor Appleton sends young inventor Tom Swift into a new gadget story in this boys' adventure book. Tom tries to build a telephone that can also send a picture, so that a caller can be seen as well as heard. His father doubts the idea at first, but Tom presses on, testing, failing, and improving the device while rivals and thieves circle his workshop and his airship.

Chapters move from a man on the roof and bad news to midnight visitors, a stolen airship, a mysterious message, and a trap set with the new invention. The picture telephone finally turns the plot, saving a fortune and catching the villains. Readers get a brisk, old-fashioned inventors' tale, full of workshops, chases, and faith that a clever machine can set things right.
4551-europe-revised:
Irvin S. Cobb wrote Europe Revised as a humorous travel book, and he opens by complaining about the average guidebook. Guidebooks, he says, are over-freighted with facts, stuffed on every page, as if the author had set out to fill the thing chock-full of facts and then went and did it. Cobb offers the opposite: a traveller's eye, a joke, and a story, with facts kept firmly in their place.

He dedicates the book to his small daughter, who bade him shed a tear at Napoleon's tomb, which he gladly did because his feet were hurting. A note warns readers not to look at a picture on page eighty-one, showing him leaping into a German feather-bed, which he calls the only blot on the book. Readers get a light, funny American tour of Europe, best enjoyed as entertainment rather than as a guide.
488-she-stands-accused:
Victor MacClure recounts the trials of notorious women in this true-crime volume, drawn from authenticated sources. Murderesses, cheats, and cozeners stand in the dock, while others, accused yet acquitted in law, get a fair hearing too. A countess, a merry widow, and an arsenic case in Brittany fill the chapters.

MacClure writes with care for fact and a dry wit, warning against cheap jokes at the accused. He notes how often a case thought fresh proves long told. The book serves readers of crime history who want real trials, not legend, and a sober look at women whom justice caught or cleared.
4976-narrative-of-an-expedition-into-cen:
Charles Sturt's narrative of an expedition into central Australia opens with the continent's rivers: the Darling's sudden floods, the Murray's periodical rise, and the geology that joins them. Earlier journeys by Mitchell, Grey, Eyre, and Oxley are weighed, along with the state of the interior as known in 1828.

Sturt then leads his own party inland, seeking the heart of a continent whose plains and rivers puzzled every explorer. Fossil beds, junctions, and theories about the interior's former state fill the account. Readers get a classic of Australian exploration, written by a leader who mapped water in a land defined by its absence.
5152-one-thousand-questions-in-californi:
E. J. Wickson, professor of horticulture at the University of California, arranged this practical volume from questions farmers actually asked him. More than a thousand answers cover fruit growing, vegetables, grain and forage crops, soils, irrigation, fertilizers, livestock and dairy, poultry, and the pests and diseases of plants.

The book is not a formal treatise but a working handbook, organised so a grower can find the answer to a single problem fast. It offers a detailed picture of California farming in the early twentieth century. It still serves as a record of what orchardists and farmers needed to know as the state's agriculture grew.
5205-speeches-of-the-hon-jefferson-davis:
This volume collects speeches by Jefferson Davis of Mississippi delivered during the summer of 1858, from a Fourth of July address at sea to meetings in Portland, Belfast, Augusta, Boston. New York and an address before the Mississippi legislature complete the tour. Extracts from his Senate speeches open the book, which was printed at Baltimore in 1859.

Davis spoke as a leading Southern senator on the eve of secession, defending Southern rights and the Union as he understood it. The speeches are primary documents of the sectional crisis, and they let readers hear, in Davis's own words, the arguments that carried the South toward disunion within three years.
6124-pamela-or-virtue-rewarded:
Samuel Richardson's Pamela, or Virtue Rewarded, published in 1740, created an epoch in the English novel. Richardson, born in 1689 and died in 1761, was a printer who rose to master of the Stationers' Company. His skill as a letter-writer brought, in his fiftieth year, a commission for model familiar letters.

Connecting those letters by a story that interested him suggested Pamela's plot and fixed its epistolary form, kept in his later works. The novel follows a servant girl whose virtue is tested by her master, told entirely in letters. Richardson turns letter-writing into suspense, conscience, and social climbing.
6490-the-betrothed:
Walter Scott opens with a long 1832 note on why he chose the Crusades as his theme, and how hard that grand theme was to match in a tale. He weighs the advice of friends, the pull of a great name, and the risk of falling short of what readers might dream up. The note sets a modest, self-aware tone for the romance that follows.

The tale itself turns on vows, honor, and love tested by war and by time apart, as its people move through a world shaped by faith and feud. Scott fills the scenes with knights, courts, and hard choices, yet keeps the heart of the matter close to home. It is a slow, stately romance of duty held against desire.
6624-ancient-china-simplified:
Edward Harper Parker, professor of Chinese at Manchester, sets out ancient China in plain form for readers new to the field. His preface opens with Boswell's remark to Dr. Johnson that English history, told short and without groundwork, would seem hardly credible. Parker takes the hint, and gives his tale the groundwork it needs.

A Chou tripod from 812 B.C., kept safe in a temple on Silver Island, fronts the book as a sign of China's long art and craft. Dynasties, sages, and wars follow in clear order. Ancient China Simplified is a useful, early primer, made to open a vast past to English readers.
6719-the-earth-trembled:
E. P. Roe's The Earth Trembled, volume fifteen of his works, opens with Mary Wallingford, love's agony, and Uncle Sheba's experience. Mara, past and future, a new solace, and two questions follow, with fireside dramas, a fair duellist, and a chivalrous surprise ahead. The chapter list promises a long, emotional tale.

Love, loss, and faith shake the characters as surely as any quake, and Roe's earnest, moral voice guides them through. His readers of the day loved his blend of romance and Christian comfort. The Earth Trembled is a sincere, period novel of hearts tested and, at last, steadied.
6757-fanny-the-flower-girl-or-honesty-re:
Selina Bunbury tells of Fanny, a flower girl of perhaps eight, who cries come, buy my flowers, fresh and fair, through the streets. With a neat basket, a white cloth to shade the blooms, and a bunch offered to each passer-by, she hopes for a buyer. Some pass rudely on, some smile, some call her a nice child, but few buy.

Honesty, as the title promises, is at last rewarded, and other tales follow Fanny's own. Bunbury writes for young readers with a moral warmth typical of her day. Fanny, the Flower-Girl is a tender, old-fashioned tale of a poor child whose good heart wins through.
6866-the-story-of-siegfried:
James Baldwin tells the story of Siegfried for his children Winfred, Louis, and Nellie, opening when the world was in its childhood. Men then saw every thing on earth, in air, or in water as alive like themselves, and every sight and sound as caused by an intelligent being. All men were poets in ideas and speech, though few wrote poetry.

Saxon cold and Greek sun shaped those fancies in different ways, north rugged and bold, south refined and clear. Baldwin retells Siegfried's dragon, sword, and doom in simple, noble prose. The Story of Siegfried is a fine, child-friendly gateway to northern myth.
71008-the-poems-of-winthrop-mackworth-pr:
A choice of the poems of Winthrop Mackworth Praed fills this book, printed at London in 1886. Frederick Cooper wrote a first word on the poet's life and work. The list of parts opens with a set of tales in verse and tales of old lore. The Red Fisherman stands at its head. Tales of the Drachenfels, of a house of the fiend, and of a tree that is dogged by a ghost come in its train.

More verse of tale and jest fills the book: a bridal at Belmont, a tale of Don Carlos in his own words, and bits on wedlock and the lone man. Songs from The Troubadour, a talk by a tutor of a school, and a walk in the old Greek mode show the range of the poet.
7788-blindfolded:
Earle Ashley Walcott's Blindfolded opens in a city of hills, with houses crowning lower heights. Bare half-mountains stand behind, ships lie in the stream, and yellow-gray water fills the bay. Its thirty-one chapters promise a mystery tale of danger, cries for help, and changed names.

Later headings run from a night at Borton's and Mother Borton's advice through a deal in stocks. A chase in a storm and the heart of the mystery follow, to the end of the journey and a reward. Through markets, mazes, and foreign lands, a hero gropes blindfolded toward a truth others hide.
8087-a-fountain-sealed:
Anne Douglas Sedgwick, author of The Little French Girl and Tante, set this novel in a Boston drawing room looking out on a wintry street. Three people sit in a room made austere by books on white shelves, a Donatello cast, bronze vases of roses, and a portrait of a commanding old gentleman in uniform. Photographs of young women fill the room, hinting at a family history that the novel slowly unlocks.

Sedgwick writes about marriage, family loyalty, and the secrets that seal themselves off from speech, which is what her title suggests. The novel's interest lies in character and atmosphere rather than incident. For readers of early twentieth-century domestic fiction, it offers a refined, psychologically attentive portrait of Boston society.
8102-the-forme-of-cury-a-roll-of-ancient:
The Forme of Cury, a roll of ancient English cookery compiled about 1390 by the master-cooks of King Richard II, is one of the oldest English cookbooks. Presented afterwards to Queen Elizabeth by Edward, Lord Stafford, and later owned by Gustavus Brander. It appears here with notes and a copious index or glossary, plus a manuscript of the same age and subject. Its motto, from Martial, praises ingenious appetite.

The roll's recipes show a medieval court kitchen at work: spiced meats, pottages, and sauces far richer than modern fare. Food historians treasure it as a source for ingredients, methods, and the language of cooking. For cooks and readers alike, it is a delicious window onto a royal table six centuries ago.
8117-the-possessed:
Fyodor Dostoevsky's novel The Possessed, also called The Devils, appears here in Constance Garnett's 1916 translation, in three parts. Its chapters move from an introductory provincial society through matchmaking, the sins of others, and a cripple, into nights of conspiracy, a duel, and Pyotr Stepanovitch's busy intrigues. The second part ends on the eve of a fete, and the third follows the fete to its disastrous end and a romance ended.

The novel is Dostoevsky's furious study of revolutionary nihilism in a Russian town, where ideas become possession and talk turns to murder. Its characters, the liberal Stepan Trofimovitch, the magnetic Stavrogin, and the scheming Pyotr, remain among his most disturbing. It is a long, dark, and prophetic book, essential for readers of Russian literature and political fiction.
8188-the-mysterious-key-and-what-it-open:
Louisa May Alcott wrote this short novel around a prophecy in old English text: Trevlyn lands and Trevlyn gold. Heir nor heiress e'er shall hold, undisturbed, till, spite of rust, truth is found in Trevlyn dust. The story opens with a young wife finding her husband Richard Trevlyn poring over the yellow. Time-worn page for the third time, laughing at its poetry while he smiles and puts the book aside. The key of the title, and what it opens, drive the mystery.

Alcott, famous for Little Women, here tries a gothic tale of inheritance, secrets, and family honour. The novel is brief and melodramatic, with a heroine's curiosity leading to buried truth. For Alcott readers, it is a charming lesser-known work, showing her range beyond domestic realism.
8207-the-philosophy-of-the-plays-of-shak:
Delia Bacon published The Philosophy of the Plays of Shakspere Unfolded in London in 1857, with a preface by Nathaniel Hawthorne, author of The Scarlet Letter. Her thesis, which she presents as a discovery, is that the plays attributed to Shakespeare encode a philosophy belonging to Francis Bacon and his circle, hidden beneath the surface text. The volume opens with aphorisms, including Lord Bacon on knowledge broken inviting further inquiry, and quotations from Love's Labour's Lost and The Tempest.

Bacon's book founded the Baconian authorship controversy, though scholars have not accepted its claims. Its importance is historical: it shows how nineteenth-century readers wrestled with Shakespeare's genius and sought a learned author behind it. For students of the authorship debate, it is the original statement of a theory that still circulates.
8379-shakespeare-s-bones-the-proposal-to:
C. M. Ingleby wrote this 1883 essay against digging up Shakespeare. A proposal to move the poet's bones from Holy Trinity Church, Stratford, and to examine them for clues to his portraits, had stirred debate, and Ingleby answers it with learning and indignation. He weighs what bones could actually prove about a face, and what the church's own records say.

To make his case, Ingleby collects instances of visits of the living to the dead, exhumations and reburials through history, and asks what reverence owes the grave. The essay defends leaving Shakespeare undisturbed, in the church where his famous curse on moving his bones still stands. It remains a spirited brief for respect over curiosity.
9333-johnny-bear-and-other-stories-from-:
Ernest Thompson Seton wrote these animal stories from Lives of the Hunted, opening with Johnny Bear. Johnny, a queer little cub, lives with his mother Grumpy near the Fountain Hotel in Yellowstone Park. A syrup tin keeps him happy for a long time, while the hotel steward's garbage draws the bears near.

Tito, the coyote who learned how, follows, with her brood and her race for life. A final tale tells why the chickadee goes crazy once a year. Seton writes from close watch of wild life. The book remains a classic of animal tales, tender, true, and full of woodland wit.
9830-the-beautiful-and-damned:
F. Scott Fitzgerald wrote The Beautiful and Damned in 1922, his novel of Jazz Age wealth and waste. Anthony Patch, a young heir, and his siren Gloria move through New York parties, kisses, and radiant hours. Book one follows Anthony, a portrait of a siren, and a connoisseur of kisses. Book two turns to the radiant hour and the slow wreck of fortune.

Fitzgerald traces how money, drink, and beauty corrode a marriage that began in glamour. His prose glitters with wit and ache. A reader gets a defining novel of the 1920s, where the beautiful learn the price of their shine.
a-face-illumined:
Edward Payson Roe builds his long novel around Ida Mayhew, whose face gives the book its title and its first chapter. The contents promise an artist's freak, a Parthian arrow, spite, reckless words and deeds, and glimpses of tragedy. An artist hero and the fashionable world around a country resort supply the stage.

Across some fifty chapters Ida moves from vanity and wounded pride toward a steadier, brighter self, while the artist who first slighted her learns to see her truly. Roe, a minister turned novelist, was among the most read American authors of his day. His tale mixes romance, moral trial, and religious feeling in the manner his readers loved.
a-fountain-sealed: Anne Douglas Sedgwick writes a fountain sealed in a Boston drawing room. The room, empty and undecorated, holds books, a Donatello cast, bronze vases of roses, and a portrait of a commanding old gentleman. Winter outside contrasts with a nearly tropical warmth within. Sedgwick builds a novel of family, art, and hidden feeling from this opening scene.
a-handbook-to-the-works-of-browning-6th-: Sutherland Orr gives a handbook to the works of Robert Browning in this sixth edition. Written at the request of members of the Browning Society, it began as a primer and keeps a primer's brevity. Orr explains Browning's poems and his indifference to general sympathy. The handbook guides readers through a difficult poet with clear notes.
all-things-considered: Gilbert Keith Chesterton considers all things, from the case for the ephemeral and Cockneys and their jokes to the fallacy of success and running after one's hat. The essays turn small topics into large arguments, defending the everyday against fashion and solemnity. Chesterton's paradoxes and good humour make the collection a lively entry to his thought.
american-lutheranism-vindicated: Samuel Simon Schmucker defends American Lutheran teaching in this book, which looks at the Lutheran symbols and disputed points, with a reply to critics. Put out in Baltimore, it backs a mild, American form of the faith against strict claims about creeds. It is a key text in the rows of the 1800s over what it meant to be Lutheran in the United States.
ancient-china-simplified:
Edward Harper Parker, professor of Chinese at the Victoria University of Manchester, simplifies ancient China for Western readers, and opens his preface with Boswell and Dr. Johnson on the strangeness of compressed history. His first chapter fixes the opening scenes: dated history, a China of small fiefs along the Yellow River, and no knowledge yet of South or West Asia.

Ninety-nine short chapters move through dynasties, philosophers, wars, and the slow knitting of the empire, with maps of rivers and shifting capitals along the way. Parker worked from Chinese sources in translation checked against originals, as his preface explains. The book gives beginners the main road through three thousand years without drowning them in names.
anson-s-voyage-round-the-world-the-text-: Richard Walter's account of Anson's voyage round the world appears here with the text reduced, introduction, notes, and glossary by H. W. Household. The voyage follows Anson's circumnavigation, its storms, prizes, and hardships, in a form cut for school and general readers. The reduced text keeps the adventure while easing the original's bulk.
bird-neighbors-an-introductory-acquainta:
Neltje Blanchan wrote Bird Neighbors as a first acquaintance with one hundred fifty birds found in gardens, meadows, and woods near American homes. Blanchan arranged her birds for beginners: by family, by habitat, by season, by size, and above all by color, so a flash of red or yellow leads straight to a name. Naturalist John Burroughs added an introduction praising the plan.

Descriptions stress what a walker with an opera glass can actually see: markings, song, habits, and haunts. Blanchan, who also wrote popular nature books as a Doubleday editor's wife and author, keeps the tone friendly rather than scientific. The book belongs to the great birding revival that taught city readers to look up.
blindfolded:
Earle Ashley Walcott wrote Blindfolded, a San Francisco mystery novel told in the first person by a young man sent west on a risky errand. Walcott drops his narrator into fog, bay water, and strange orders from the start. A cry for help and a change of name pull him in deeper.

Stock deals drive much of the plot, with chapters on a day in the market and a flutter in prices. Doddridge Knapp, Mother Borton, and her daughter Luella shape the hero's path, now helping, now warning. A den, a chase in a storm, and a battle in a maze raise the stakes. The last chapters bare the heart of the mystery and pay the hero his reward. Readers who like market intrigue get both.
branded:
Francis Lynde published Branded with Scribner's in 1917, and Grosset and Dunlap reprinted it in 1918 with a frontispiece by Arthur E Becher. Lynde tells the tale in the first person, through a bank clerk arrested in his own office. A promise to Agatha Geddis starts his fall.

Chapter heads trace the brand: the heating of the iron, the searing touch, prison as Number 3126, then a westward fresh start. A plain-clothes man dogs the ex-convict who seeks honest work. Paper walls, a broken wagon, and a hold-up test the new life. A woman's love and a reckoning clear the way to restoration on the mountain's top. Lynde writes a western-flavored plea for the man who has paid and wants work.
britannica-1911-abated: Abated is the headword of a very short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives the word as an old technical term in masonry and metal work. It applies to parts sunk below the surface of the work. Inscriptions supply the plain case: the ground is sunk round the letters, so the letters or ornament stand out in relief. The whole notice runs to two lines, fixing one workshop sense of a common word for readers of old building and craft accounts in the 1911 edition.
britannica-1911-abu-hamed:
Abu Hamed is a town of the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, set on the right bank of the Nile and reached by rail from Khartum. The 1911 Britannica entry places it at the centre of the great S-shaped bend of the river. From Abu Hamed the railway to Wadi Halfa cuts straight across the Nubian desert, near the older caravan route to Korosko.

Railways shape the rest of the account. A branch line runs down the right bank of the Nile to Kareima in the Dongola district. The town's name comes from a celebrated sheikh buried there, whose tomb was so respected that desert travellers left goods beside it, trusting its sanctity to keep them safe.
britannica-1911-achenwall-gottfried:
Gottfried Achenwall (1719-1772) was a German statistician born at Elbing in East Prussia. He studied at Jena, Halle, and Leipzig, taking his degree at the last. He then removed to Marburg. For two years he lectured on history there. He also taught the law of nature and of nations. At Marburg he began his inquiries in statistics. Those inquiries made his name known.

A professorship at Gottingen followed in 1748. He stayed there until his death. His chief works all dealt with statistics. That was the systematic description of states. His account of Europe's leading constitutions appeared in 1749. Revised editions followed in 1762 and 1768. They kept his name attached to the young science.
britannica-1911-ainger-alfred:
Alfred Ainger (1837–1904) served London's Temple Church for close to forty years, first as reader and at last as master. Born in the capital, an architect's son, the English churchman and writer read at King's College, London, and at Trinity College, Cambridge. Orders came in 1860, then a curacy at Alrewas and a post at the Sheffield Collegiate School. His tie to the Temple began in 1866.

Ainger became master of the Temple in 1894, after Dr Vaughan. He held a canon's stall at Bristol too, and served as chaplain to Queen Victoria and King Edward VII. Soft wit and a giving heart won him a wide ring of friends. In books his name rests most on his warm grasp of two writers, Charles Lamb and Thomas Hood. His own works count volumes on Lamb and on Crabbe, plus editions of the Essays of Elia and of Lamb's Letters.
britannica-1911-akbar-jellaladin-mahomme:
Akbar, Jellaladin Mahommed (1542–1605), was one of the greatest and wisest of the Mogul emperors. He was born at Umarkot in Sind on 14 October 1542. His father, Humayun, had been driven from the throne a short time before by the usurper Sher Khan. After more than twelve years in exile, Humayun won back his rule. He held it for a few months only, and then he died. Akbar took his father's place in 1556.

Akbar ruled at first under the regency of Bairam Khan, a Turkoman noble. Bairam's force in beating back rivals to the throne, and his harsh hold on the army, did much to firm the new-won empire. But Bairam was by nature a despot, and a cruel one. When order was in part set right, Akbar saw that he must take the reins in his own hands.
britannica-1911-albinus-bernhard-siegfri:
Albinus, Bernhard Siegfried, a German anatomist of 1697 to 1770, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His family name was originally Weiss. Born at Frankfort-on-Oder, where his father held a chair of medicine, he followed that chair to Leiden in 1702. There he studied under Boerhaave and Bidloo, two of the age's leading medical teachers.

A year in Paris deepened his work in anatomy and botany under Vaillant and Winslow. Recalled to Leiden in 1719 as lecturer on anatomy and surgery, he succeeded his father in that professorship two years later. He soon ranked among Europe's most famous anatomy teachers, drawing practising physicians as well as students to his classroom. In 1745 he moved to the professorship of the practice of medicine. His brother Frederick Bernhard succeeded him in anatomy, and another brother also won distinction.
britannica-1911-aldred:
Aldred, also spelled Ealdred, died in 1069 after a church career spent largely on state business. He rose step by step: abbot of Tavistock near 1027, bishop of Worcester in 1044, then archbishop of York in 1060. King Edward the Confessor leaned on him heavily, and he played a large part in affairs of the realm.

War and errands filled his years. He led a failed raid on the Welsh in 1046 and helped win back an earldom for Sweyn, Earl Godwin's son. Trips for the king took him to Rome, and to the emperor Henry III he went to bring home Edward, son of Edmund Ironside, from Hungary. No English bishop before him had made the pilgrimage to Jerusalem, as he did in 1058. Norman-age records credit him with crowning Harold II in 1066. After Hastings he yielded to William at Berkhampstead and crowned the Conqueror on Christmas Day.
britannica-1911-baldinger-ernst-gottfrie:
Ernst Gottfried Baldinger (1738–1804) was a German physician, born near Erfurt on 13 May 1738. He studied medicine at Erfurt, Halle, and Jena. In 1761 he was put in charge of the military hospitals tied to the Prussian camp near Torgau.

His 1765 treatise on the diseases of soldiers, De Militum Morbis, was well received. Baldinger then held chairs of medicine at Jena from 1768, at Göttingen from 1773, and at Marburg from 1785, where he died in 1804. The 1911 Britannica entry notes his famous pupils, among them Sömmerring and Blumenbach, and counts some eighty-four separate treatises from his pen, besides many journal papers.
britannica-1911-bardili-christoph-gottfr:
Christoph Gottfried Bardili (1761–1808) was a German philosopher, born at Blaubeuren in Württemberg and dead at Stuttgart. His system had little influence in Germany; Reinhold alone set it out against the attacks of Fichte and Schelling. Yet the entry holds that some of his ideas opened the way for Schelling and Hegel after him.

Bardili broke with Kant's split between the matter and the form of thought. Philosophy, he urged, should study thought in itself, pure thought, as the ground of being. Its ruling principle is identity, and logical thinking is real thinking. The 1911 Britannica entry faults his one-sided working-out of the idea, which left thought with no power of growth and in the end reduced it to counting.
britannica-1911-benett-etheldred:
Etheldred Benett (1776–1845) was one of the earliest English women geologists, second daughter of Thomas Benett of Pyt House near Tisbury. She later lived at Norton House near Warminster in Wiltshire. For more than twenty-five years she gave herself to gathering and studying the fossils of her home county.

Benett’s catalogue of the organic remains of Wiltshire went into Sir R. C. Hoare’s County History. A small number of copies were also printed as a separate book in 1831 and handed out privately. She died in January 1845, leaving a county fossil record built by one collector’s patience. The entry is short, but it marks how much of early geology rested on such local work.
britannica-1911-bernhardy-gottfried:
Gottfried Bernhardy (1800–1875) was a German philologist and literary historian. He was born at Landsberg on the Warthe in Brandenburg. Jewish parents in reduced means raised him, and two uncles paid for his schooling. He heard Wolf, Böckh, and Buttmann at Berlin University. He took his doctorate there in 1822. By 1829 he held the chair at Halle and directed its philological seminary.

His chief works were outlines of Greek and Roman literature. The Roman outline reached a fifth edition in 1872. The Greek prose part of his Greek outline never appeared. He also wrote a Greek syntax and edited the lexicon of Suidas. That edition ran from 1834 to 1853. He died suddenly at Halle in 1875.
britannica-1911-berwick-upon-tweed:
Berwick-upon-Tweed is an English market town, seaport, and county in itself, at the mouth of the Tweed. It stands on the river's north bank, 339 miles north by west of London. The 1911 Britannica entry gives 13,437 people in 1901. The East Coast rail route to Scotland passes through it. The town keeps a rare prize: a complete ring of ramparts. Earth faced with stone, with bastions and a dry ditch, they date from Elizabeth's reign.

Older lines from Edward I's time survive in part as well. In 1905 the Board of Works took charge of those ruins as national relics. The parish church and guild hall get notice in the article. Trade in local farm produce and the Tweed salmon fishery anchor its past. A bridge crossed the Tweed here in very early times, the entry adds.
britannica-1911-bone-bed:
Bone bed is a geology term for a layer rich in bones, and the entry sorts its loose and strict uses. Loosely it covers any stratum holding bones, and also the bone-bearing rubble found on cave floors. Strictly it names thin layers of bone scraps that sit on clear, traceable levels in the rock record.

The Ludlow Bone Bed is the star example. It lies at the base of the Downton Sandstone in the Upper Ludlow series, and two such beds at Ludlow stand about 14 feet apart. Though thin, the bed can be followed 45 miles into Gloucestershire, made almost wholly of spines, teeth, and scales of ganoid fish. A second famous bed, the Bristol or Lias Bone Bed, holds fish and saurian remains in dark shales above the Keuper marls.
britannica-1911-bruneau-alfred:
Alfred Bruneau (born 1857) was a French composer born in Paris to parents devoted to music. Brought up to play the cello and educated at the Paris Conservatoire, he played in Pasdeloup's orchestra and soon began composing, writing a cantata, Genevieve de Paris, at an early age. An heroic overture of 1884 and choral symphonies followed.

Opera made his name. His first, Kerim, was produced in 1887, and in 1891 came the successful Le Reve, its libretto founded on Zola's story. Another Zola subject gave L'Attaque du moulin in 1893, and Zola himself wrote libretti for Messidor in 1897 and L'Ouragan in 1901, a partnership that defines his stage work. A Requiem of 1896, two song collections, and the Legion of Honour in 1895 fill out the record, and his music criticism in several volumes is praised for literary quality and vigour.
britannica-1911-capus-alfred:
Alfred Capus (1858–) was a French author and playwright. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career to date. He was born at Aix, in Provence, on 25 November 1858. He trained as an engineer, then turned to journalism. In 1878 he published a volume of short stories. He wrote it with his partner L. Vonoven. A one-act play by the pair followed in 1879. In 1894 Capus joined the staff of the Figaro.

His novels of those years follow young men starting out. Qui perd gagne appeared in 1890, and Faux Départ in 1891. From the first he drew his first comedy, in 1894. The entry lists his stage successes year by year. They include Innocent, Rosine and Mariage bourgeois. Les Maris de Léontine and La Veine came in 1900 and 1901. Notre Jeunesse, in 1904, reached the Théâtre Français first among his plays. Later pieces were written with Arène and with Descaves.
britannica-1911-cellier-alfred:
Alfred Cellier (1844–1891) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English musical composer born at Hackney. From 1855 to 1860 he was a chorister at the Chapel Royal, St James's. Arthur Sullivan was a colleague there. He became organist at All Saints, Blackheath, in 1862. In 1866 he took charge of the Ulster Hall concerts in Belfast. He returned to London in 1868 as organist of St Alban's, Holborn.

Cellier conducted at theatres in Manchester and London through the 1870s. He composed many comic operas and operettas in those years. His great success came with Dorothy in 1886. It opened at the Gaiety theatre and ran, across three theatres, until April 1889. His setting of Gray's Elegy was heard at the Leeds Festival of 1883. The entry owes much of his manner to Sullivan's influence, while crediting him as a fertile melodist of elegance and refinement. He died in London in December 1891.
britannica-1911-fleckeisen-carl-friedric:
Carl Friedrich Wilhelm Alfred Fleckeisen (1820-1899), German philologist and critic, was born at Wolfenbuttel on 23 September 1820. He was educated at the Helmstedt gymnasium and the university of Gottingen. After several teaching posts he became vice-principal of the Vitzthum Gymnasium at Dresden in 1861. He held that post until he retired in 1889. He died on 7 August 1899, after a life given to Latin texts and school work.

Fleckeisen is known chiefly for his labours on Plautus and Terence. In knowledge of those authors he was rivalled only, perhaps, by Ritschl, his lifelong friend. His Exercitationes Plautinae of 1842 won praise as a masterly study of Plautus's language. He published an unfinished edition of Plautus's comedies and a new edition of Terence in 1898. In his editions he tried to restore the text by his research on Latin usage and metre, and he cared greatly about spelling.
britannica-1911-flugel-johann-gottfried:
Johann Gottfried Flugel (1788-1855), German lexicographer, was born at Barby near Magdeburg on 22 November 1788. He began as a merchant's clerk, but emigrated to the United States in 1810 and made a special study of the English language. Returning to Germany in 1819, he was appointed lector in English at the university of Leipzig in 1824. In 1838 he became American consul. He also served as representative and correspondent of the Smithsonian Institution and other leading American bodies.

Flugel's fame rests on his Complete English-German and German-English Dictionary, first published at Leipzig in two volumes in 1830. It circulated widely in Germany, England and America alike. J. Sporschil assisted him in the work. A new, enlarged edition, edited by his son Felix Flugel, appeared at Brunswick in 1890-1892, with further editing by Professor Immanuel Schmidt. The entry thus honours a dictionary maker whose book served readers on both sides of the Atlantic for generations.
britannica-1911-frewen-accepted:
Accepted Frewen (1588-1664), archbishop of York, was born at Northiam in Sussex. He was educated at Magdalen College, Oxford, becoming a fellow in 1612. The college let him serve as chaplain to Sir John Digby, envoy in Spain. A sermon he preached at Madrid pleased Prince Charles. On taking the throne, Charles made Frewen one of his chaplains.

He became canon of Canterbury in 1625 and president of Magdalen in the following year and twice served as vice-chancellor. Through his work the university plate was sent to the king at York in 1642. Made bishop of Lichfield and Coventry in 1644, he lost his estates under Parliament in 1652. He fled to France, since the warrants named him Stephen Frewen by mistake. At the Restoration he was made archbishop of York in 1660 and chaired the Savoy conference of 1661. The hosted file also holds neighbouring entries.
britannica-1911-lacroix-antoine-francois:
Antoine François Alfred Lacroix (1863– ), French mineralogist and geologist, was born at Mâcon on the 4th of February 1863. He took his doctorate of science at Paris in 1889. In 1893 he became professor of mineralogy at the Jardin des Plantes, and in 1896 director of the mineralogical laboratory in the École des Hautes Études. His special subjects were minerals tied to volcanic action and igneous rocks, the effects of metamorphism, and mineral veins, studied in many parts of the world, notably the Pyrenees.

He wrote much on the mineralogy and petrology of Madagascar for scientific journals. His large volume La Montagne Pelée et ses éruptions (1904) covered the Martinique eruptions, and his Minéralogie de la France et de ses Colonies appeared in 1893–1898. He also worked with A. Michel Lévy. In 1904 he was elected to the Académie des sciences.
britannica-1911-meshed:
Meshed, rightly Mash-had, which means the place of martyrdom, is the capital of the province of Khorasan in Persia. It stands in a plain fed by the Kashaf-rud, a stream that feeds the Hari-rud. The city lies 460 miles east of Teheran and 200 miles north-west of Herat. It stands 3,800 feet high. Its people number about 70,000 who stay, and 10,000 more who come and go. Those who come and go are pilgrims to the shrine of Imam Reza.

The town is of no set shape and runs about six miles round. A mud wall with towers rings it. In the south-west corner stands the citadel, set in a wall 25 feet high with a broad dry ditch. The ditch is 40 feet deep in parts and can be filled with water from streams nearby. The city has five gates.
britannica-1911-shed:
Shed has two main senses, and the article traces both. As a noun, it means a small hut, shelter, or outhouse. It can have a shed roof, or lean-to, with one set of rafters that fall from a high wall to a low one. The word is also used for a large roofed shelter, open at the sides. Such sheds store goods, rolling stock, or engines on a railway or dock wharf.

Skeat links the noun to shade and shadow, from an old root that means to cover. As a verb, shed means to spill, scatter, or cast off. Its first sense seems to have been to part or divide, a sense that lives on in watershed. The old English verb was sceadan, to divide or separate. Some scholars hold that the verb of spilling is a distinct word, tied to a Frisian word for shake.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adrian-hamste:
Adrian Hamsted founded the Adrianist sect, born at Dordrecht in 1524, who died at Bruges in 1581. Nothing is known of his personal history, and very little is known of the short-lived sect that took his name. The Adrianists, mostly women, professed Anabaptist doctrines in general.

Their specific beliefs cannot be ascertained. Charges of immorality were named against them, but those charges were never proved. The short entry thus records a sect chiefly by its founder's dates, its Dordrecht birthplace, and its general Anabaptist colour, leaving its particular doctrines wholly unknown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostles-cree:
The Apostles' Creed is a short formula of twelve articles, or statements, holding the fundamental tenets of Christian belief, traditionally assigned to the twelve apostles as authors. Through the Middle Ages most believed the apostles, on Pentecost day, composed the creed together, each contributing one article. That legend dates to the sixth century and is foreshadowed in a sermon attributed to Ambrose, which notes the creed pieced together by twelve separate hands.

About the year 400 Rufinus gave a fuller account, saying he received it from earlier ages. He described the creed as the joint work of all the apostles deliberating together, though he does not assign each article to one apostle. The long article tests legend against early evidence, tracing how a baptismal summary grew into the familiar text. Readers learn both what the creed says and why its apostolic authorship cannot be taken at face value.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-john-: John Speed, an English layman also called Spence, was put to death at Durham on 4 February 1594 for helping the priest John Boste, whom he guided between Catholic homes. He refused offers meant to make him conform, and died firm in his faith. Grace Claxton, condemned with him, was spared for a time because she was expecting a child. Speed was later beatified in 1929 among the Durham Martyrs, while Boste was canonized in 1970.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coenred:
George Hind's entry follows Coenred, also called Cenred or Kenred. He was king of Mercia from 704 to 709. As son of King Wulfhere, he was likely too young to rule when his father died in 675. His uncle Aethelred took the throne first. Coenred became king of the Southumbrians in 702. Two years later he gained all Mercia, when Aethelred retired to a monastery.

A reaction against his people in 709 pushed Coenred to give up the throne to his cousin Coelred. He then traveled to Rome with Offa of the East Saxons. There Pope Constantine gave him the monastic habit. Peace loving and pious by temper, he seemed better suited to the cloister than to kingship. Bede's account, quoted here, tells how he befriended the exiled Saint Wilfrid and tried to turn one of his nobles toward a better life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-creed:
A doctrinal entry untangles the word creed, from the Latin credo, I believe. In general it means the whole body of beliefs held by a religion. More narrowly it means a summary of the chief articles of faith professed by a church or community, such as the Apostles', Nicene, and Athanasian creeds.

The entry explains the Latin term symbolum, a sign or collection, marking those who share a belief. It distinguishes a creed from a profession of faith, enjoined on special occasions, and from Protestant confessions like Augsburg and Basle. The principal Catholic creeds are then surveyed in turn, with their history and use, and a bibliography of standard works closes the piece.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-discalced:
Discalced, from Latin words meaning without shoes, marks religious congregations whose members go wholly barefoot or wear sandals. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces the custom in the West to Saint Francis for men and Saint Clare for women. After the Franciscan rule was reshaped, the Observants kept the barefoot way, followed by the Minims and Capuchins.

The Discalced Franciscans, also called Alcantarines, formed a distinct branch until 1897 and wore no footwear at all. Followers of Saint Clare began barefoot and later wore sandals. The entry then lists later barefoot groups, from the Discalced Carmelites of 1568 to the Passionists, each marked by this visible sign of poverty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-the-be:
George the Bearded, Duke of Saxony from 1500 to 1539, ruled a well-ordered duchy while resisting Luther. Born at Dresden in 1471 to Albert the Brave, he was groomed for the Church and better educated than most princes, serving as regent in 1488 while his father fought in Friesland. Married to Barbara of Poland in 1496, he succeeded his father in 1500 and took Friesland in 1505, selling the troubled province to Burgundy in 1515 for one hundred thousand florins.

At home George split the duchy into districts, curbed robber-knights, and reordered the courts, sometimes at cities' expense. At first not opposed to Luther, he turned as the Reformer's aim grew clear, and Luther reviled him in bitter letters. Though alive to church abuses, George stood Catholic, joining his Lutheran son-in-law Philip of Hesse and cousin Frederick in 1525 to crush the peasants' revolt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hatred:
Hatred, a vehement aversion toward a person or toward something bound up with that person, is split by theologians into two kinds with very different moral weight. Loathing fastens first on a person's qualities and only secondarily on the person. Hostility aims straight at the person, delights in his discredit, and wishes his lot unmixedly hard.

Hostility breaks charity directly and is always sinful, sometimes gravely. Loathing of what is evil is no sin and may even be virtuous, as in praying for a harmful heresiarch's death to stop his ravages, provided spite does not hide behind zeal. Hatred of God himself, loathing his perfections precisely as God's, stands at the head of sins, a diabolical turning of the will that even mortal sin only implies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicene-creed:
The Nicene Creed, approved in amplified form at Constantinople in 381, is the Christian faith's statement common to the Catholic Church, all Eastern Churches separated from Rome, and most Protestant bodies. Soon after Nicaea, new faith statements arose, mostly changes to the Nicene Symbol against new phases of Arianism. At least four appeared before Sardica in 341, where a new form was presented but not accepted.

The Nicene Symbol remained the sole formula among faith's defenders, gradually recognised as the right statement of faith for those seeking baptism. Its change into the Nicene-Constantinopolitan formula now in use is usually ascribed to Constantinople. Chalcedon in 451 called it the Creed of Constantinople's council of 381, reading it twice into its Acts. Socrates, Sozomen and Theodoret omit this, though they record the remaining bishops backing Nicene faith after the Macedonians left.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-tunsted:
Simon Tunsted, English Minorite born at Norwich, died at Bruisyard, Suffolk, in 1369. Joining the Greyfriars at Norwich, he won distinction for learning and piety and became a doctor of theology. He held several weighty church offices. He served as warden of the Franciscan convent at Norwich, regent master at Oxford in 1351, and provincial superior of his order in England in 1360.

He is also the reputed author of the Four Principal Things of Music, a clear and valuable medieval treatise. Davey shows it is certainly not the work of Hanboys or Tewkesbury, though the case for Tunsted is admittedly insufficient.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-aelred:
St. Aelred, abbot of Rievaulx, homilist, and historian, lived from 1109 to 1166, and this entry follows an Englishman who chose the cloister over a king's court. Son of a married priest of the kind common in eleventh- and twelfth-century England, born at Hexham, he knew David, St. Margaret's youngest son and soon King of Scotland, at whose court he served as a sort of page to Prince Henry.

David loved the pious youth, advanced him, and wished him a bishop. But Aelred became a Cistercian at the new abbey of Rievaulx in Yorkshire. Where as master of novices he was long remembered for tenderness and patience Sent with twelve monks to found Revesby in Lincolnshire in 1143, he later ruled Rievaulx itself as abbot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-baldred:
St. Baldred was a Celtic bishop of Strathclyde, born about 643 and dead at Aldhame in Haddingtonshire about 607, though the entry warns the chronology is obscure. This entry follows a man said to have been the immediate successor of St. Kentigern, or Mungo, founder of the Glasgow see. Like Kentigern, he was of Irish ancestry, but he counts as a British saint, since Strathclyde was part of Britain.

The best authorities on Scottish history agree Baldred was born towards the middle of the sixth century. Before his consecration he laboured for many years in Strathclyde. He founded numerous houses for monks and for holy virgins, besides the churches of Aldhame, Tyinguham, and Preston Kirk. The kingdom's disturbed state forced him, after a short rule, to retire from governing the Strathclyde Britons, as his predecessor had been.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-elined:
Elined, virgin and martyr of about 490, survives mainly through a hilltop church and a pilgrim feast. Daughter of Bragan, the British prince behind Brecknock's name, she rejected an earthly prince's marriage to wed herself, in Giraldus Cambrensis's words, to the eternal King. Her church stood on a hill near Aberhodni castle, and throngs visited it on her feast, 1 August, when many miracles were reported. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 names Giraldus as chief authority.

William of Worcester says she was buried at Usk, and the Bollandists judged the evidence for her cult sound. Churches across Wales bore the names of Bragan's children, Elined's among them. The entry is short, but it preserves a Welsh devotion: a princess, a refusal, a martyrdom, and a hillside shrine crowded once a year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-athanasia:
One of the Church's approved symbols of faith, given a place in her liturgy, is examined here in full. Short and sharp, the Athanasian Creed sets out the doctrines of the Trinity and the Incarnation, with brief mention of other dogmas. It states and restates its two central truths in varied forms, so that the three Persons of God and the two natures in the one Person of Christ stand unmistakable.

Its origin, date, and authorship are weighed, since Athanasius himself almost certainly did not write it. The Marquess of Bute's English translation is printed entire, beginning Whosoever will be saved, and the entry notes the creed's warnings to those who reject its articles. Liturgical use in East and West closes a compact guide to a demanding text.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-blessed:
