Public honour paid to the holy dead is sorted into two grades in this entry, and the line between them is drawn with precision. Some saints are beatified, others canonized. Beatification permits public worship in certain places and for certain acts only. In recent discipline the pope alone can grant it, though bishops once bestowed it on martyrs and heroes of virtue.

Early local permissions, spreading from church to church with episcopal sanction, grew into a universal precept from the Roman pontiff. While honour stayed local it remained beatification. Once the whole Church received it, canonization had arrived. Two marks decide the difference: a precept of public worship, and extension to the entire Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-uhtred:
Uhtred, also spelled Owtred, was an English Benedictine theologian and writer born at Boldon in North Durham about 1315. He died at Finchale Abbey on 24 January 1396. He joined the Durham Benedictines about 1332, was sent to London in 1337, and entered Durham College at Oxford three years later. There he took his licentiate in 1352 and his doctorate in 1357. He spent the next decade disputing at Oxford, often against members of the mendicant orders.

That combative record led the writer Bale to brand him wrongly as a supporter of Wyclif, a charge the entry corrects. In 1367 Uhtred became prior of Finchale Abbey, an office he held four times in all. He guided a small house on the Wear through the later fourteenth century. His writings, largely sermons and tracts against the friars' privileges, are listed with care, offering a portrait of a monastic scholar known more for argument than for system.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-walkenried:
Walkenried was formerly one of Germany's most celebrated Cistercian abbeys, in the Duchy of Brunswick, lying between Lauterberg and Nordhausen. Countess Adelheid of Klettenberg founded it in 1127 and confirmed by Innocent II in 1137, its first monks came from Camp in Cologne's archdiocese. Under its first abbot, Henry I, it founded daughter houses at Pforta in 1132 and Sittichenbach in 1141.

Growing rich with lands reaching the Rhine and Pomerania, its monks devoted themselves to mining, smelting, and fishing. Decay set in during the fifteenth century, and the Peasants' War nearly destroyed it: at Easter 1525 a mob of eight hundred southern Harz peasants marched on Walkenried. The abbot and monks fled with the archives, the abbey was plundered, and its church tower torn down. Its next abbot turned Lutheran with his monks in 1546, the emperor's 1548 restoration order went unheeded, and a Protestant school opened there in 1557.
claimed:
Claimed!, by Gertrude Barrows Bennett, is a weird novel of 1920 that opens not with its hero but with a ship's log. The preface quotes the log of the Portsmouth Bell, a British merchant vessel under Captain Charles Jessamy. A seismic wave on May 14 has left the sea coated with floating scoria and ash, six to fifteen inches thick.

Compasses disagree, heat stands at 150 degrees in the coolest parts of the ship, and land is sighted near 40 degrees north, 31 degrees west. Ashore and inland, the tale turns to men, digging, and dread. An old hand, Jesse Robinson, warns a younger man that a trial is coming beside which all past trials were child's play.
dawn-o-hara-the-girl-who-laughed:
Edna Ferber's first novel, Dawn O'Hara, subtitled The Girl Who Laughed, is dedicated to her mother, who frequently interrupts, and her sister Fannie, who says sh-sh outside the door. Dawn, a New York newspaperwoman, suffers the smash-up of overwork in chapter one and is sent west to Milwaukee to recover. Mostly eggs and good-as-new chapters chart her cure.

Boarding with the German Knapf family, Dawn absorbs kaffee and kaffeekuchen and writes features. The grave Dr von Gerhard courts her. Meanwhile danger from her past gathers as the shadow of terror. Ferber drew on her own reporting years in Wisconsin. The novel's warmth and newsroom detail promised the career that produced Show Boat.
doe-osti-17084198-developing-extended-sh:
Sadhvikas Addamane and a Sandia team sought tougher infrared detectors for space surveillance in this project report, numbered 240596. Space sensors working in short wave infrared face steady damage from high energy particles, which shortens detector life. Their approach embeds tiny structures called quantum dashes, made of indium arsenide on indium phosphide, in the sensing layer.

Light output tests before and after neutron exposure showed dash samples, emitting near 2 micrometers, degrading about five times less than quantum well samples at like wavelength. Full detector structures with zero to forty dash stacks were then grown, built, and tested. Devices with dashes again held up about five times better under radiation, with normal detector performance otherwise.
doe-osti-17171705-proceedings-for-the-wo:
Ellen O'Brien, Stephanie Lyons, Tomi Akindele, and colleagues record the 2026 Workshop on Applied Nuclear Data Activities, known as WANDA, in proceedings issued by Los Alamos in July 2026. The annual meeting links groups that fund and use nuclear data, so needs and capabilities can be matched and funding aimed better.

Five topic areas structured the sessions. They covered safeguards data for advanced reactors, building an inventory sub library, the path to next generation fission data, artificial intelligence for nuclear data, and the instruments and facilities that produce data. Each session named its grand challenge, its needs, and shared themes. Recommendations close the record, including capabilities to use before they lapse and chances the field should seize.
doe-osti-2585514-tantalum-experiments-in:
David Ames of Sandia National Laboratories evaluated a set of criticality experiments for the International Handbook of Evaluated Criticality Safety Benchmark Experiments, in report SAND2025-09577R. The experiments placed tantalum in a lattice of uranium dioxide fuel rods enriched to 6.90 percent uranium-235. The rods sat in a triangular pattern with 1.02 centimeter pitch, moderated and fully reflected by water.

Benchmark files like this one give safety analysts trusted cases for testing their calculation codes. Ames documents the experiment in full detail, from the fuel array down to parts such as the cadmium base liner, so others can model it exactly. The evaluation carries the handbook identifier LEU-COMP-THERM-112. Elijah Lutz reviewed it internally, and Nicolas Leclaire of the French nuclear safety authority reviewed it independently. Sandia supported the work through the Department of Energy Nuclear Criticality Safety Program.
doe-osti-2586806-hydrogen-transportation:
Arun Veeramany of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory leads a six-author team with Sandia National Laboratories in this August 2025 seismic risk assessment. Melissa Louie, Brooke Marten, Marina Miletic, Bhavya Mamnani, and Brian Ehrhart complete the team. The setting is Portland International Airport, which is weighing a fleet of 28 fuel cell electric buses that could also supply backup power during outages.

The team assessed the pressurized piping of a generic hydrogen refueling station at the airport, the component with both high vulnerability and usable fragility data. Hazard came from Cascadia Subduction Zone earthquake rates in the literature, translated into peak ground acceleration and adjusted for soil through shear wave velocity values. For a 15-foot pipe, the yearly frequency of total pipe failure came out at 3.24 times ten to the minus eight for soft soil and 1.31 times ten to the minus eight for firm ground.
doe-osti-2586990-hydrogen-transportation:
Issued under Sandia number SAND2025-10458R in August 2025, this seismic risk assessment studies hydrogen fueling at an airport. Arun Veeramany and Brooke Marten of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory wrote it with Melissa Louie, Marina Miletic, and Brian Ehrhart of Sandia. Bhavya Mamnani is also on the team. Portland International Airport is considering 28 fuel cell buses, and the report asks how an earthquake would threaten the hydrogen supply behind them.

Only pressurized piping at a generic airport refueling station was analyzed, since fragility data exists for piping and not for the other parts. Cascadia Subduction Zone events were assumed to recur every 490 years, a conservative choice. The probability of total pipe failure in one event came to 1.59 times ten to the minus five on soft soil, with a shear wave velocity of 160 meters per second. On firm ground at 760 meters per second, the figure was 6.42 times ten to the minus six.
doe-osti-2588045-release-of-endf81sab-en:
Wim Haeck, Nathan Gibson, and Noah Kleedtke of Los Alamos National Laboratory issued this release memorandum, LA-UR-25-29086, dated August 19, 2025. It announces ENDF81SaB, a set of ACE-format data files for thermal neutron scattering, built from the ENDF/B-VIII.1 library. Thermal scattering data tell a transport code how slow neutrons bounce off atoms bound in materials such as water, ice, and metal hydrides, where chemistry changes the physics.

The package is posted for unlimited release on nucleardata.lanl.gov, alongside the library it derives from. Most of the memo is the data listing itself: file after file for each material at each temperature. Deuterium in heavy water, for example, appears at temperatures from 523.6 to 650 kelvin in fine steps, and fluorine compounds such as beryllium fluoride follow. For reactor and criticality analysts, this is the working data behind thermal spectrum calculations, delivered in the exact format their codes consume.
doe-osti-2998229-the-parabolic-wave-equa:
Anna Harden, Isaac Carter, and Jason Derr derive wave equations for radio signals crossing the ionosphere, in Los Alamos report LA-UR-25-30058, issued 9 October 2025. The ionosphere is a plasma threaded by Earth's magnetic field, and both vary with position. The team's starting point is the classic parabolic wave equation, widened to handle that variation.

Starting from Maxwell's equations with the Lorentz force law, the derivation builds the plasma's permittivity tensor and assumes its gradients stay small beside the wavenumber. Solving an eigenvalue problem splits the wave into three modes: the ordinary mode and both polarizations of the extraordinary mode, each with its own index of refraction. In the ionosphere the magnetization current vanishes, which simplifies the field equations. Next step, stated in the report, is testing the equations inside an existing scintillation code.
doe-osti-2999145-detection-of-trace-cont:
Jonathan Frank, Christopher Kliewer, Mark Johnston and co-workers at Sandia National Laboratories test laser tools for a pulsed power puzzle, in report SAND2025-12379R, printed September 2025. During a discharge, metal electrodes heat almost instantly and puff out trace gases from their surfaces. Those gases can seed plasma and drain power. Catching a whisper of gas beside a flashing discharge, in place and in the moment, is the hard part.

The team tried laser-induced fluorescence for hydrogen atoms and hydroxyl radicals, and laser photofragmentation for water vapour, in a model foil discharge rig. Plasma light swamped all three, and none gave a clear signal. A new method, femtosecond degenerate four-wave mixing, suppressed the interference and did detect hydrogen atoms. A few shots showed large signals near the metal surface, hinting at a wave of hydrogen leaving the foil. The work proves one workable route toward routine contaminant watching.
doe-osti-2999378-expansion-and-update-of:
Hoyoung Kwon, Xinyu Liu, Thomas Sykora and co-workers at Argonne National Laboratory document an update in ANL/ESIA-24/23 to the R&D Feedstock Carbon Intensity Calculator. The calculator sits inside R&D GREET 2025, Argonne's life-cycle model for fuels and vehicles. It scores how much carbon each crop or biomass feedstock carries before it ever reaches a fuel plant, a figure that decides which biofuels count as low-carbon.

The 2025 round expands feedstock coverage and refreshes farm data. One visible change aligns nitrous oxide factors, a potent greenhouse gas from fertilised fields, with the IPCC 2019 Tier 1 values across all feedstocks. For canola, the factor for synthetic nitrogen rose from 1.04 to 1.374 percent, and for nitrogen in canola residue from 0.94 to about 1.26 percent. Farming energy per metric ton of spring canola fell from 528,667 to 438,891 British thermal units. Tables give the new inputs crop by crop.
doe-osti-3001074-preliminary-analysis-of:
Nicolas Stauff, Jia Zhou, W. Neal Mann and colleagues from three national laboratories survey whether nuclear plants should power data centres in ANL/NSE-25/47, dated 31 August 2025. Data centre demand is surging with artificial intelligence. The report projects United States data centre energy use rising by 24 to 74 gigawatt-years by 2028, needing 27 to 85 gigawatts of installed capacity if nuclear supplied it all. Hyperscale and large colocation sites dominate that appetite.

Chapters size the demand, inventory the current nuclear fleet and recently retired plants as candidates, and weigh reactor options from big light-water units to small modular designs. Technical coupling, economics and social and environmental effects are each examined, drawing on the recent wave of industry announcements pairing reactors with server farms. The analysis is preliminary by design: a map of scenarios and open questions, meant to guide the Systems Analysis and Integration campaign rather than pick a winner.
doe-osti-3002329-proceedings-for-the-wor:
Jesse M. Brown, Ellen O'Brien, Todd Bredeweg, and editors from eight institutions compile the proceedings of a 2025 workshop in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/3966, dated August 12, 2025. The workshop covered applied nuclear data: the measured and evaluated numbers, such as reaction cross sections, that reactor and safeguards calculations consume. Contributors came from national laboratories, Brookhaven, and the University of California at Davis, among others.

Proceedings gather the talks and working sessions so non-attendees can use them. Topics in the reference trail include data platforms run by the Energy Department and the International Atomic Energy Agency, and data science for nonproliferation. Applied data work is unglamorous but load-bearing: every simulation in this field inherits the quality of these numbers. The volume records where the community sees gaps and what it plans to measure next.
doe-osti-3003996-the-national-diagnostic:
D. Bradley of Lawrence Livermore documents a national planning effort in report LLNL-TR-2013707, dated November 2025. It is the National Diagnostic Plan for high energy density science, current as of September 2025. High energy density experiments, at facilities like the National Ignition Facility and the Z machine, depend on diagnostics: cameras, spectrometers, and imagers that record extreme, fleeting events.

The plan inventories diagnostic systems and sets multi-year priorities. Tables lay out timelines from fiscal 2026 to 2030 for the Nuclear Imaging System, including calibration automation and detector upgrades. Other sections cover neutron imagers and spectrometers for magnetic direct drive fusion, and the readiness of local diagnostics on the OMEGA laser. Revisions against the 2024 plan are flagged at the front. Facility planners across the complex use it to sequence investments.
doe-osti-3005844-deployment-of-digital-t:
Christopher Perullo of Turbine Monitoring and Support Services leads a project reported under DOE award DE-EE0011043, submitted August 6, 2025. The project ran from January 2024 to March 2025, with Savannah State University and the Electric Power Research Institute. It built a digital twin for an aging hydro turbine fault: looseness between the rotor's spider arms and its rim, called rotor rim float.

Undetected rim float can tear up a generator's rotor and stator. The twin is a virtual sensor: it predicts the float signal from ordinary existing sensors, avoiding costly dedicated instruments. Utility historical data trained the models, and a market study checked fleet-wide demand. Savannah State's forecasting trials with random forest and gradient boosting methods looked promising. The report closes the award with the twin's design and its limits stated.
doe-osti-3007678-towards-machine-learnin:
Final report for DOE grant DE-SC0024678, by Benjamin Holtzman of Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory with partners at MIT and the Planetary Science Institute, covers phase one of a geothermal fracture project. The long-term goal is a machine-learned constitutive model, a rule set linking stress, heat, and fluid flow to how rock cracks.

Laboratory thermal-cracking experiments at MIT supplied the training evidence, with acoustic sensors listening to tiny cracking events. Careful cataloguing mattered: at a low detection threshold the catalogue held 271,744 events with near-random timing, while a stricter threshold kept only 213 strongly clustered events. Any learned model must know which catalogue it learned from.
doe-osti-3007897-design-and-optimization:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2025/4052, by Matthew Frost and Thomas Huegle, dated December 2025, designs a proposed NB2 guide system for the Cold Guide Hall at the High Flux Isotope Reactor. Neutron guides are mirrored channels that carry cold neutrons from the reactor to instruments down the hall.

Simulations ran in the McStas ray-tracing toolkit, with monitors at each guide section recording spatial distribution, phase space, and wavelength spectrum. Extra drift distance before the sample lets structure in the beam smooth out, at some cost in divergence and losses. The resulting beam suits a neutron radiography or small-angle scattering test setup, and the design leaves room for future instruments.
doe-osti-3012497-using-low-cost-bio-deri:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2025/4368 documents a project led by Katie Copenhaver, with Matt Korey and Amber Hubbard, working with Bergey Windpower. The team tested whether recycled and plant-derived materials could replace standard materials in small and medium wind turbine blades. They kept Bergey's own fiber layouts and shop methods so the results would apply to real production.

Two alternative resins, a recyclable epoxy and an infusible thermoplastic, matched the standard resin well in strength, stiffness, heat behavior, and fatigue tests. Recycled glass fiber mats failed as a substitute: they drank up far more resin, adding weight and cost, and reacted with epoxy to form a porous foam. The resins look viable for future blades, while the foam reaction may suit sandwich panels instead.
doe-osti-3015389-informing-transmission-:
NLR/TP-6A40-97167, dated January 2026, forecasts transmission supply chains from national grid studies. Rose, Fuchs, Ramirez, and Pandian wrote it. Grid plans mean little if factories cannot supply the steel, aluminum, transformers, and converter stations. The team thus turned grid expansion cases for 2025 to 2035 into part and material demand.

For new lines alone, the AC case needs 1,626 thousand tons of aluminum and 318 thousand tons of steel. The multi-terminal case needs 1,973 and 386 thousand tons. The analysis details demand for transformers too. It includes a proposed 4,000 megawatt HVDC bipole converter transformer design. It also tracks trends in unit weight per megavolt-ampere. Results are meant to warn policymakers and manufacturers where bottlenecks will form first.
doe-osti-3016947-establishment-of-a-vert:
AvCarb LLC of Lowell, Massachusetts, prepared this report for award DE-EE0011353, dated February 6, 2026. Cynthia Lemay Olson was principal investigator, and Iryna Zenyuk and Sirivatch Shimpalee were among the technical contacts. The project period ran from January to October 2025. Its goal was a fully domestic, vertically integrated process for making substrates used in gas diffusion layers for fuel cells.

Work began with a baseline evaluation of carbon products, sampling along and across the web of material. Partner universities supplied physical property data, X-ray tomography scans, and fuel cell performance curves for a product called MB-30 on three carbon veil designs. One lesson stands out: future gains need the microporous layer and catalyst layer tuned together with each substrate design. The report maps a United States supply chain for a part fuel cells cannot do without.
doe-osti-3017703-tex-chlorine-assemblies:
Eric Aboud, Konner Casanova, and Paul Maggi of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, with Jesse Norris also named on the record, wrote this July 2025 report, LLNL-TR-2002677. It documents the TEX-Chlorine assemblies, a benchmark experiment series. The assemblies stack plates of highly enriched uranium with sodium chloride absorbers, using polyethylene as moderator and reflector, on the Comet assembly machine.

Chlorine is a strong neutron absorber, and its nuclear data need measured checks. The report gives the full description safety reviewers require: the setup, the design, and the machine's fixed platform. Later sections work through errors in dimensions and materials. Simulation comparisons use the MCNP code with modern evaluated data files. Criticality safety analysts get a fully specified benchmark, the kind that anchors the computer predictions used to keep real operations safe.
doe-osti-3020530-local-resource-assessme:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5600-96003, by Anne E. Corrigan, Vanessa Mathews, and Georgina Davis, sizes up a resource created by an infestation: spruce trees killed by beetles across Alaska. The assessment was produced for the Denali Commission. Dead spruce could supply local biomass energy, but only if enough salvageable wood stands near the communities that would use it.

The team combined aerial detection survey data on beetle damage with state forest inventory records. Inventory polygons overlapping the beetle-kill layer were summed to estimate biomass, an approach that deliberately captures the broadest extent of usable material, including stands next to confirmed damage. The report explains the method's limits, including survey flight coverage. Results give the Commission and local planners a defensible estimate of feedstock for wood-energy projects.
doe-osti-3021907-hydrogen-transportation:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory final report PNNL-38178 for CRADA 555, by Arun Veeramany, Brooke M. Marten, Feng Pan, and co-authors, dated September 2025, studies a two-for-one resilience idea at Portland International Airport. The Port of Portland is considering 28 fuel cell electric buses. The hydrogen station built to fuel them could double as an emergency energy asset, keeping airport operations alive through large-scale power outages.

Working with Sandia, the team assessed whether the bus mission and the backup mission can share one hydrogen system, and what risks that creates. One dedicated analysis treated earthquakes. Using site-specific seismic hazard data and pipe fragility models borrowed from the nuclear industry, it quantified failure risk across the airport's soil conditions, softer near the Columbia River. The report frames hydrogen's versatility as the selling point for other airports weighing similar projects.
doe-osti-3022474-collaborative-center-fo:
A final report for DOE award DE-SC0020233, by Igor Adamovich, Yiguang Ju, and Bruce Koel, closes out a joint center on plasma-assisted combustion and catalysis. The center studied how nanosecond-pulse and hybrid plasmas create reactive species that can ignite fuels at low heat, speed oxidation, and drive chemistry such as ammonia synthesis over catalyst surfaces.

Twelve research threads are summed up, from time-resolved measurements of radicals and vibrational populations to 2D imaging of methyl concentrations by laser-induced fluorescence. Plasma-catalytic ammonia making and nitrogen oxidation in hybrid discharges get fuller treatment, as does a heated supersonic plasma flow reactor built for spectroscopy. One notable finding is a possible thermal-chemical instability. In it, plasma kinetics and low-heat fuel oxidation feed back on each other, and a uniform discharge breaks into streamers.
doe-osti-3024495-estimation-of-radiation:
Ricardo S dos Santos Augusto of Brookhaven National Laboratory estimates the radiation fields that lost injection beam would create at the Electron-Ion Collider's rapid cycling synchrotron. His note is BNL-229585-2026-TECH, dated March 2026. J P Saraiva and C W Schaefer are co-authors. When injected beam misses its mark, the stray particles shower in the machine and nearby material takes a dose. Designers need those numbers before shielding and access rules can be set.

Variants covered electron beams at 5, 10, and 18 GeV with their matching current settings. One downstream scenario stayed mild, with absorbed doses reaching at most 0.3 rad per hour, while a detector placed in the shower's path caught much more. Radiation damage estimators are reported too, as high-energy hadron fluence and silicon 1 MeV neutron-equivalent fluence for the most conservative case.
doe-osti-3024717-resstock-measure-docume:
Jes Brossman and Yingli Lou of the National Laboratory of the Rockies document a ResStock upgrade package in report NLR/TP-5500-96281, dated March 2026: advanced air sealing combined with drill-and-fill wall insulation. Crews drill small holes in existing walls, blow in insulation, and seal the leaks that make old houses drafty. ResStock modelers need the measure defined exactly so national savings estimates stay comparable.

Input tables list the choices the measure accepts, from wall types such as wood stud, log wall, straw bale, and structural brick to a wall assembly R-value entered as a number. Applying the insulation changes some heating and cooling arguments in the EnergyPlus model too, because better-insulated houses need different equipment capacities. The authors warn that their variable list is not exhaustive.
doe-osti-3029879-longitudinal-twiss-para: Twiss parameters got tilt-measured, and this DOE text studies phase space ellipses. The pages detail the longitudinal findings. The physicists get their data. The ellipses were phase space. The data were physicist. The tilted were ellipses. The space were phase.
doe-osti-3030034-resstock-measure-docume:
Yingli Lou and Sinoun Phoung of the National Laboratory of the Rockies document a combined retrofit in report NLR/TP-5500-96347, dated April 2026. The note belongs to the ResStock series, which models energy upgrades across the United States housing stock. This package joins three measures at once: advanced air sealing of the home shell, attic floor insulation, and duct sealing with insulation. Each part cuts a different leak path for heated or cooled air.

Option lists show the modeled ranges. Air sealing spans tightness levels from 7 to 50 air changes per hour at test pressure. Ceiling insulation runs from none to R-49, with the top value used only outside the warmest climate zone. Duct choices pair leakage shares of 10, 20, or 30 percent with insulation from none to R-8.
doe-osti-3030035-resstock-measure-docume:
Yingli Lou, Sinoun Phoung, and Jes Brossman of the National Laboratory of the Rockies document a four-part home retrofit in report NLR/TP-5500-96349, dated April 2026. The note belongs to the ResStock series, which models upgrades across the United States housing stock. The package joins advanced air sealing, attic floor insulation, and duct sealing with a fourth step: drill-and-fill wall insulation, blown into closed wall cavities through small drilled holes.

Modeled across the stock, the package cut total site energy use by 27.2 percent. The note explains how to pull results for homes that got some or all four steps. Four data columns flag which homes received which measure, and an enumeration dictionary for the release defines each column and its allowed values.
doe-osti-3363907-thermal-rgb-and-multisp:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4607, by Chad Melton and Andrew Duncan, documents a drone imaging campaign from November 2025. Cameras flew over inert unexploded ordnance placed in fields at Norris and Georgetown, Tennessee. Three campaigns collected 23,004 images, about 76.2 gigabytes, using color, thermal, and limited multispectral sensors on Skydio X10 and Wingtra aircraft across summer and winter.

Flights ran hourly during daylight over tall grass, short grass, and gravel. Review of the imagery showed ordnance stood out most when sunlight was changing fast. The best windows were roughly 10 to 60 minutes after sunrise and 20 to 60 minutes after sunset. Minutes right after clouds broke long heating also worked. Those moments sharpen thermal contrast between metal and ground. The dataset gives detection researchers realistic field imagery, with the caution that all ordnance was inert.
doe-osti-3364359-distinguishability-of-r:
West Virginia University's final report for DOE award DE-SC0020269, led by Mark E. Koepke, covers a U.S. contribution to the TJ-II stellarator program in Spain from 2018 to 2021. The physics question: do particles and heat leak out of a fusion plasma together, or can each move on its own? The answer shapes whether stellarator confinement can be predicted and controlled. Partners included Spain's CIEMAT fusion laboratory and Russia's Kurchatov Institute teams.

The project combined a new baffled probe design for edge measurements with advanced fluctuation analysis of existing data. Bispectral analysis showed the geodesic acoustic mode, a plasma oscillation, trading energy with broadband turbulence, with key quantities about 180 degrees out of phase. Separating particle flux from energy flux experimentally gives modelers a harder test to match.
doe-osti-3366083-metadata-standards-for-:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-24484, by Mark Offtermatt, Kathryn Gregonis, Camille Mathieu, and co-authors, sets extended metadata field standards for the NSE, the laboratory's digital collection environment. Catalog records are only as findable as their fields, and this volume recommends additional fields and data representation rules beyond the core standard. Each field gets a full treatment.

Chapters work through Description, Subject, Type, Format, and Notes fields one at a time. Every entry pairs best-use guidance with future opportunities, telling catalogers not just what to write but why the practice matters. Standards consulted are listed up front. For an archive ingesting thousands of technical reports, consistent extended fields decide whether a searcher finds the right document or drowns in near misses.
doe-osti-3367033-augmenting-llm-based-ag:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4611, by Aaron Werth, Gary Hahn, Raymond Borges Hink, and six co-authors, tests whether language-model agents can help attack and commission industrial control systems. The same agent that penetration-tests a plant network might also help operators configure it. Critical infrastructure needs both capabilities tested safely before adversaries improvise their own.

The June 2026 study augments LLM-based agents with tools and context for operational technology work, then measures their performance on pentesting and commissioning tasks. Findings speak to where agents already help, where they stumble on protocol specifics, and what guardrails matter when the target is live infrastructure rather than a capture-the-flag game. Utilities and labs weighing AI assistants for control systems get evidence instead of vendor claims.
doe-osti-3367795-advanced-techniques-for:
Saint-Gobain final technical report for DOE award DE-EE0009394, by Kameron Conforti and Julie Godefroid with Georgia Tech, covers August 2021 to July 2025 work on drying gypsum with less energy. Wallboard plants burn large fuel volumes driving water from gypsum slurry; the project attacked the dryer's energy input from the slurry side, studying how the material spreads, sets, and releases water.

One thread checked why measured yield stress disagreed with spreading behavior: setting during measurement and shear-history effects were tested and ruled out, leaving inertia in the spreading flow as the standing explanation. The December 2025 report pairs rheology with drying trials. For an industry where dryers dominate plant energy bills, small percentage savings scale across millions of boards.
doe-osti-3374944-robust-heat-flux-sensor:
A final report for Department of Energy award DE-FE0031902, by Oded Rabin of the University of Maryland, closes a sensor project that ran from January 2021 to December 2025. The report was filed on March 31, 2026. Its subject is heat-flux sensing inside coal-fired boilers. Boiler walls face flame, ash, and sharp heat swings that kill standard gauges. Operators still need wall heat readings to run plants well and spot trouble early.

The team built sensors on the transverse Seebeck effect, where heat flow across a slanted crystal makes a voltage. One design uses elemental antimony. A second, built for hotter duty, uses elemental rhenium. Bench calibration showed the output rose in a steady, monotonic way with heat flux. Papers on both designs appeared in sensor journals during the award.
doe-osti-3377470-building-energy-analysi:
Technical report NLR/TP-5600-99889, dated June 2026, models energy use in two Juneau, Alaska housing types: manufactured homes and multifamily blocks. Conor Dennehy, Milena Levey, Jeff Maguire, and Anne E. Corrigan ran the study at the National Laboratory of the Rockies. Juneau's cold, wet winters make heat the dominant cost. The team asks what air-source heat pumps save against plain electric heat, month by month.

One worked case is a four-unit block. On plain electric heat it uses 20,275 kilowatt-hours a year, at 2,490 dollars. With heat pumps the same block uses 14,186 kilowatt-hours, at 1,757 dollars. The yearly saving comes to 733 dollars. Gains bunch in the cold months: January and December show the largest drops. Summer months save almost nothing, since little heat runs then. Full tables let housing staff test their own blocks against the same math.
doe-osti-3409787-techno-economic-analysi:
Ally Pantaleo Acquaviva of the National Laboratory of the Rockies wrote report NLR/OT-5600-100407, dated August 2026, on energy options for Crow Creek, Alaska. Remote sites like Crow Creek often burn costly diesel for power. Solar panels and batteries were weighed against that base case.

With solar and storage added, life-cycle costs fell below the diesel base case at the load studied. Fuel savings and avoided diesel costs outweighed the higher build cost. Net savings of 30,529 dollars over the project life are cited at one panel price. Village planners get a grounded case for mixing solar into a diesel grid.
doe-osti-3427062-release-of-eprdata25-en:
Los Alamos document LA-UR-26-27338, by Wim Haeck and Michael Aaron Lively and issued August 13, 2026, releases eprdata25, a data set for photon and electron transport. The files rest on the ENDF/B-VIII.1 nuclear data library. ACE format files feed Monte Carlo transport codes.

File lists pair each element's photoatomic, electron, and atomic relaxation data. Hydrogen, helium, and lithium open the list in order. A template stamps each file with the release name and date. Code users gain a fresh, matched set of atomic data for radiation transport work in medicine, shielding, and research.
doe-osti-3682475-surrogate-process-devel:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2026/4746, dated August 2026, develops stand-in processes for a coated particle fuel pellet design. Six authors are printed: Alicia M. Raftery, Henry Osborne, Ryan Heldt, Eddie Lopez Honorato, and Tyler Gerczak among them. In the design, boron absorber particles are coated, then packed inside an oxide fuel pellet. The coat gives helium room and shields the absorber. Stand-in materials let the team test making steps without real fuel.

Cold-flow tests pushed irregular zirconium diboride particles through five nozzle shapes. A single-inlet, five-outlet nozzle gave the steadiest spout and wall flow, and was picked for later coating work. Overcoating trials used cerium dioxide powder over zirconia spheres as stand-ins. A steady process window was found at a set mix ratio. But the dried feedstock had weak strength and a split size spread. Pellets pressed from it cracked more as packing rose.
doe-osti-3682535-initial-characterizatio:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2025/4216, dated September 2025, gives first results on material harvested from Ringhals Unit 2 in Fiscal Year 2025. Nine authors are printed, led by Samantha Sabatino, Xiang (Frank) Chen, and Paula Bran Anleu. One half of the report covers unirradiated concrete cores from the plant. The other half sums up cutting stainless steel welds from the unit.

Concrete cores were scanned, sliced, polished, and cut into thin sections. Stones pulled from one core were sorted for close study of their makeup. Element maps show how key elements spread through a slice. A partner workshop is proposed to split roles among Oak Ridge, Vattenfall, and other groups. The aim is a shared base for judging radiation effects on old plant concrete.
doe-osti-3685199-mapping-and-bridging-ba:
University of Michigan's final technical report closes a project on how knowledge about solar farms moves through rural towns. Michael Craig, an assistant professor, was principal investigator. The project ran from June 1, 2021 to May 31, 2025. Big solar plants often land in rural areas, where land is open and cheap. Whether they get built turns on zoning. Under a quarter of regional ordinances even addressed such projects.

Four work areas structure the report. The first gathered data on knowledge flows, money effects, and trusted local voices. The second built computer models of solar's effect on rural economies and of future build-out under zoning limits. The third tested ways to share findings with towns. The fourth spread results to stakeholders. One model result stands out: silent ordinances cut solar build sharply, while clarifying them restores nearly all of it. Michigan and Wisconsin took the steepest cuts.
doe-osti-3686267-implementation-of-machi:
Argonne report ANL/LWRS-26/1, dated August 2026, builds machine learning tools to read steam generator tube inspection data. Four authors are printed: Thomas Elmer, Xin Zhang, Alexander Heifetz, and Sasan Bakhtiari. Eddy current probes scan the tubes for wear and cracks. Array probes now return far more data than hand review handles well.

The team widened its flaw library and built a synthetic data generator to train the models. The generator shifts flaw place and traits, swaps tube sizes, and adds varied noise and backgrounds. Three network types were scored: a plain multilayer network, a convolutional network, and a residual convolutional network. Each section reports how well its model finds and sizes damage. A side thread studies learning from few examples. That route could catch odd flaws that rule-based systems tend to miss.
doe-osti-3708661-targeted-extraction-of-:
A June 2026 final report to the Department of Energy closes award DE-EE0009494, led by David Jassby at the University of California, Los Angeles with Princeton as partner. The team built an anaerobic electric membrane bioreactor for city wastewater. The system treats the water while pulling out useful products: fatty acids, ammonia, and phosphate.

Bench work matured each part, then a lab system joined electric fermentation, gas stripping membranes, and treatment membranes. A field unit ran at the Hyperion plant in El Segundo, California. The ammonia membrane used cheap stock materials and reached top-class flux rates. A layered membrane split acetic acid from water with a strong separation factor and low energy use. Cost and life-cycle checks ran beside the lab work. Seven journal papers came out of the project, which the report says met its goals on budget.
doe-osti-3818591-in-process-monitoring-f:
A final report dated June 30, 2026 closes award DE-EE0009399 for the Edison Welding Institute, led by Alex Kitt. Partners were GE Research, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and Lockheed Martin. The project built watch gear for electron beam printing of titanium parts. Printed parts today face costly scans after the build to hunt hidden flaws. The team instead watched heat during the build itself. A thermal camera and a dual-wavelength pyrometer tracked melt pool and layer temperatures.

Both sensors landed within a few percent of contact gauge readings. Feeds from all sensors were aligned onto shared maps of test blocks. Software then sorted build stretches into quality classes, from clean runs to seven kinds of process upset. The aim was to flag suspect zones so later scanning could shrink. Contract delays ended the project early, in March 2026. The first two budget periods met their milestones; the third went unfinished.
doe-osti-3818603-providing-opportunities:
Prize rules from the Department of Energy's Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation govern the PROSPECT planning prize. No author is named; entries close October 5, 2026. The prize tackles a workforce crunch across the critical minerals supply chain. Mining program enrolment has fallen forty-five percent since 2015. Fewer than three hundred mining graduates finish nationwide each year. Every link of the chain, from mines to recycling plants, reports the same staff shortage.

Entrants submit education plans that grow the pipeline of trained graduates and credential holders. The stated aim is to double that output by the end of 2027 and 2028. Reviewers score each plan from zero to six across weighted tests. Plans must show how they add to, not copy, support already in place. Teams file through the HeroX platform and sign a truth statement under penalty of perjury.
ester-ried:
Pansy tells a conversion story in Ester Ried, published at Boston by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard, illustrated by Elizabeth Withington. Ester keeps house in a long, wide kitchen with no end of things to do, and no rest in sight. Her sister Sadie watches her curiously, glimpsing some strange change, as the pictured caption has it.

Twenty-eight chapters carry Ester through a Sunday lesson, a journey, cousin Abbie's household, and a strange Christian. The little card Ester hides in her Bible marks the turn, when company waits downstairs and Maggie calls her. Crosses, tested faith, and God's way fill the later chapters, to At Last. Isabella Alden, writing as Pansy, made the Ried family a household name in Sunday schools.
europe-revised:
Irvin S. Cobb wrote Europe Revised as a guidebook that boasts of containing no facts. Cobb warns readers that guidebooks are over-freighted with information and promises relief. His dedication credits his small daughter, who bade him shed a tear at Napoleon's tomb. His feet, he explains, were hurting him there anyway.

Chapters sail the Atlantic, survive German feather-beds, and tour the capitals of the old world. Cobb treats seasickness, stewards, and steamer trunks as the true subjects of travel. His humour is broad, good-natured, and deliberately unreliable. Every assertion, he notes, may readily be controverted by post. The book sends up the American tourist while remaining one itself. Readers who want Europe's jokes rather than its dates will find Cobb a companionable fraud of a guide.
exposition-of-the-apostles-creed:
Dodds's Exposition of the Apostles' Creed walks through the creed article by article. James Dodds was a minister and Doctor of Divinity. A quote from Luther's Table-Talk fronts the contents. Luther there confesses he still studies the creed, the commandments, and the Lord's Prayer daily.

The book follows the creed's twelve articles in order. Article 1, on God the Father Almighty, is split into five short sections. Later articles cover Christ's birth, suffering, death, and resurrection. The descent into hell and the ascension each get close reading. Final articles treat the Holy Ghost, the church, forgiveness, and resurrection of the body. Dodds writes for readers who want each clause explained plainly.
fanny-the-flower-girl-or-honesty-rewarde:
Selina Bunbury's Fanny, the Flower-Girl, or Honesty Rewarded, with other tales added, is a moral story for young readers. It opens with little Fanny, perhaps eight years old, crying her fresh flowers through the streets, basket on arm and clean cloth shading her nosegays.

Passers-by smile, admire the child, or pass rudely on, but few buy, and Fanny patiently rearranges her bunches after each disappointment. The tale rewards her honesty and perseverance, as its subtitle promises, and the added stories carry the same gentle moral tone. Readers who collect Victorian tales for children, or who want a period picture of street selling, will find Fanny sweet, short and sincerely meant.
finished:
H Rider Haggard's Finished, dated from Ditchingham House in May 1917, completes the Zulu trilogy begun in Marie and Child of Storm. Allan Quatermain meets Anscombe in Natal, falls in with the sinister Dr Rodd and Miss Heda, and is drawn again to the dwarf Zikali's kraal. The contents promise a valley of bones, a great council, and war.

Cetewayo receives Quatermain, the madness of Nombe breaks out, and the road leads to Isandhlwana, where the British camp is destroyed; the middle chapters cross the Ivuna and Black Umfolozi toward Ulundi. Haggard blends his invented hunter's adventures with real history he had witnessed as a young Natal official. Finished closes his Zulu saga in elegy.
friends-though-divided:
Henty sets this novel at the start of the English Civil War. Two Oxford school friends face the split in July 1642. Harry Furness follows his father, a colonel for the king. Herbert Rippinghall takes the Parliament side from his family. Both boys swear their friendship will survive the war.

The chapters follow battles, escapes, and prison breaks. Harry serves on missions and defends outposts under fire. The story reaches the execution of King Charles. It moves on to Drogheda, a sea fight, and Worcester. Kidnapping and slavery in the Bermudas widen the scene. Henty mixes boyhood adventure with the war's main events. The friends' divided loyalty holds the plot together.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BaldwinEd_Baldw: nsia-BaldwinEd Baldwin Ed: the made public government document on Ed Baldwin, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item. From the archive shelves, for readers of the collection.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BrunerFred_Brun: FBI Teletype, Dallas to Washington, October 16, 1967: the bureau's teletype to Assistant Director Rosen - the body text garbled. A damaged capture, preserved as found, for researchers and readers. A US government document from the archive. A worthwhile addition to the shelves.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CallawayTed_Cal:
Harold Weisberg summarized the Warren Commission testimony of Ted Callaway, given March 26, 1964, and printed at volume 3, pages 351 to 357 of the hearings. Callaway was a Dallas car salesman who witnessed the aftermath of Officer J. D. Tippit's murder.

Callaway heard five shots, then saw a man with a raised pistol cutting across Patton Avenue, and hollered at him as he passed. His account helped fix the gunman's flight from the Tippit scene toward the Texas Theatre. Weisberg's summaries were working tools, distilling testimony he believed the commission had mishandled, and this one is preserved from his files.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-EpsteinEdwardJa:
Edward Jay Epstein reported for The New Yorker in its A Reporter at Large series on February 13, 1971. His subject was the Chicago police raid of December 4, 1969, in which Black Panther chairman Fred Hampton was killed. The article's title asks a hard question: The Panthers and the Police: A Pattern of Genocide?

Epstein examined the raid as part of a wider pattern of police action against the Panthers. Hampton's death had already become a national controversy over how the raid was planned and carried out. The piece preserves a major magazine's close reporting on that fight, written while the case was still unfolding.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIHeadquarters: An internal FBI memorandum lists Oswald file serials drawn from headquarters tickler files, the Bureau's reminder system for pending matters. The serials named are 1212, 4920, and 4993. The text is garbled. A folder label notes the material was received by Mark Allen on October 25, 1985. The memo survives mainly as an index of file numbers rather than a readable account.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KennedyJohnFMey:
A dialogue-format piece titled Flashbacks: Ambushed by the Harvard Squares stages a strange request. Timothy Leary, the LSD advocate, is asked to instruct an unnamed important man in the use of the drug. The man is implied to be connected to Mary Pinchot Meyer and to President Kennedy. The publication that printed the piece is not identified.

Dialogue pieces let writers say in theater what they could not prove in prose. Meyer, a Washington figure later murdered, has long been tied to Kennedy in print. The piece preserves that rumor culture in dramatic form, a period artifact of the psychedelic and political undergrounds meeting.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KennedyJusticeV: Victor Navasky wrote about Robert Kennedy under a double description: as Attorney General, and as his father's son. His subject within that frame is James Landis, the former dean and presidential adviser whose fall Navasky calls a strange, sad tale. The surviving record gives the author and the titles but no date, so the piece stands as Navasky's study of Landis under Kennedy.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ReggabMohamed_R: Mohamed Reggab names this declassified US government document in the Internet Archive's holdings. The entry is bare - no year, no department, no precis. Public text unlocated. For now it is a name attached to a government file.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Ag:
Agustín Edwards owned El Mercurio, Chile's most powerful newspaper, and backed the 1973 coup against Salvador Allende. Agustin Edwards: A Declassified Obituary writes his life again from the secret record.

An ordinary obituary repeats a public reputation. A declassified one can add what the files show: Edwards's dealings with the CIA and his role in the campaign against Allende's government. The briefing book uses his death as the moment to publish that record. For readers of Chile's history, it corrects the polite version of a media magnate's life with documents.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Ch:
Peter Kornbluh edited this National Security Archive briefing book, number 642, published on October 5, 2018. It marked thirty years since Chilean voters rejected General Augusto Pinochet in the historic 1988 "NO" vote. That vote ended his dictatorship and opened the way back to democracy.

Declassified United States documents in the posting showed that Pinochet had planned a violent second coup to keep his powers if he lost. Santiago's Museum of Memory and Human Rights added those documents to its permanent exhibition on the restoration of democracy. The record ties a dictator's secret plan to the public memory of how he fell.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cold-war:
Henry Kissinger served as national security adviser and secretary of state, and few American officials left a more argued-over record. This National Security Archive posting presents a declassified dossier on that record. It uses his initials, HAK, the shorthand his own staff used.

A dossier built from declassified paper lets readers judge the controversies from documents rather than from memoirs or attacks. The posting's value is that grounding: claims about Kissinger's diplomacy, secrecy, and wars can be checked against what the files actually say. The documents, rather than the legend, are allowed to speak first.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia_Red:
Black bars hide the words in nearly every declassified file, and this posting, dated April 2019, studies those bars themselves. Over the years the National Security Archive collected hundreds of examples of dubious secrets. Those are places where the hidden text seemed to protect embarrassment, not security.

Redaction is where openness and secrecy meet on the page. Comparing what was blacked out with what later came out shows how often caution, habit, or self-protection drove the censor's marker. For any reader of declassified records, the file is a field guide to reading the gaps as evidence too.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_henry-ki:
In the mid-1970s South Korea quietly pursued a nuclear weapons capability, including a French reprocessing plant. This briefing book, posted in April 2019, draws on recently declassified documents from the Ford administration. Henry Kissinger's State Department pressed Seoul hard on the contract.

Washington insisted that the South Koreans break their contract with France for the plant. Reprocessing produces plutonium, the material of bombs, so the plant was the heart of the dispute. The documents show an ally being forced to back down in private. They also show how much of nonproliferation diplomacy happens as quiet pressure, not public treaty talk.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
The President's Daily Brief is the short intelligence summary written for the president each morning. James E. David edited this briefing book, posted in December 2016, on what filled those briefs in the 1960s and 1970s. Two topics appeared more than almost any others.

Soviet missile and space programs were among the most frequent subjects briefed to the president. That frequency is itself a finding: it shows where American anxiety sat during the Cold War, in rockets and orbits. A run of daily briefs lets readers watch the arms race through the one document the president was sure to see.

For years the Soviet Union beamed microwaves at the American embassy in Moscow, and the reason stayed mysterious. Peter Kornbluh and William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in September 2022. It opens a declassified series on the Moscow Signals, including projects code-named PANDORA and BIZARRE.

The posting appeared on the fifth anniversary of the CIA pulling agents out of Cuba over the Havana Syndrome illnesses. That timing is the argument: an older case of unexplained signals and sickness may inform a newer one. The documents give the Moscow episode, long treated as Cold War folklore, a proper paper record at last.

Secrecy And Leaks: When The US Government Prosecuted The Press - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers. Deserves a place on the shelf.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_195:
Freshly declassified State Department documents, posted in August 2017, confirm how the 1953 Iran coup began. In late 1952 the British Foreign Office approached the Truman administration more than once. London proposed a coup to overthrow Iranian Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddeq.

Two previously top secret memoranda from senior State officials describe the communications and meetings that began in October 1952. British officials worked to win American support for the plot. The coup itself came in August 1953, under a new president. These papers settle the question of who first brought the idea to Washington, and when, in the plotters' own record.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_japan-nu:
For the first time, in a declassification noted here in February 2016, the United States government officially admitted a Cold War fact long reported by others. American nuclear weapons had been stored on Okinawa, the Japanese island that hosts major United States bases. Photographs bearing on the story had been available since 1990.

Official admission matters even when a fact is widely believed. Okinawa's nuclear history sits inside a larger argument about bases, Japanese anti-nuclear feeling, and secret agreements between allies. A formal declassification moves the subject from allegation to record, and gives Japanese and American readers a shared documentary starting point.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
In January 1965 Harvard professor Henry Kissinger met top Israeli officials and came away nearly certain of something Israel denied. He told American diplomats in Tel Aviv that Israel had begun a nuclear weapons project. This briefing book, posted in November 2020, publishes that meeting record for the first time.

Its title names the twin themes: duplicity and self-deception around the American inspections of Israel's Dimona reactor in 1964 and 1965. Visits meant to verify a peaceful program were managed by the hosts and half believed by the visitors. The record lets readers watch both sides perform a check that neither side fully trusted.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p: Soviet Politburo Discussed Billion-Dollar Spy: the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Taint: Tainted Trove: the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete, a single capture, dated material, filed, an obscure item. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers. On the library shelves.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_iran_New_document:
In 1953, Iran's elected prime minister, Mohammad Mosaddeq, was overthrown in a coup backed by Britain and the United States. An October 2019 National Security Archive news post covers a documentary that retells that story: Coup 53, directed by Taghi Amirani and edited by the famed film editor Walter Murch.

The filmmakers built the movie from recently uncovered documents and fresh interviews, and some of those documents come from the Archive's own collection. A coup once denied or blurred has become provable on paper, and the film shows the paper on screen. For readers, the posting connects two kinds of work the Archive does: prying records loose, then watching artists turn those records into a story the public will actually sit through.
helen-with-the-high-hand-2nd-ed:
Arnold Bennett called this light novel an idyllic diversion. The copy here is a new edition issued in 1915. Helen, a young widow with a mind of her own, comes back into her uncle's quiet life. She soon takes charge of his house, his meals, and his plans.

Short chapters track teas, calls, cooks, and small plots. Helen schemes to marry off her mother and to bend her uncle's habits. Bennett keeps the tone dry, warm, and amused throughout. Readers who like gentle comedy of manners will enjoy watching Helen win each small round.
his-majesties-declaration-defended:
John Dryden wrote this pamphlet in 1681, in the form of a letter to a friend. Charles the Second had dissolved two parliaments in quick order. His declaration gave his reasons, and a hostile pamphlet attacked it. Dryden answers that attack point by point.

The hosted copy is a 1950 scholarly reprint, with an introduction by Godfrey Davies. Dryden argues over addresses, votes, and who may stand near the king. His prose is sharp, close, and scornful of weak logic. Readers get a prime sample of Restoration political combat, from the age's greatest English pen.
hobson-imperialism-1902-1st-ed:
John A. Hobson published Imperialism: A Study in 1902, and this entry holds the first edition text. Hobson had reported from South Africa during the Boer War. He argues that empire grows from underconsumption at home. Workers paid too little cannot buy what factories make, so surplus capital seeks outlets abroad.

Investors, not the nation, gain from the colonies their money opens. That charge shaped Lenin's later book on imperialism and Keynes's thinking too. Hobson's mix of economics and moral attack made the study a classic. A later impression of the book is also held. The first edition shows his argument in its original force.
how-it-happened:
Kate Langley Bosher published this novel in September 1914. Carmencita, its heroine, opens by smashing a hated hat. The high-crown, narrow-brim felt hat is her Christmas present to herself, she declares: getting rid of it. Her energy sets the book's brisk, warm tone at once.

Van Landing searches the city on a rough day in later scenes. A girl tells him her small brothers and sisters are bound to have Christmas. His search has humanized the sordid streets for him, Bosher writes. Sardines with lemon and toasted cheese season the talk. Readers get a Southern Christmas tale of pride, poverty, and unexpected grace.
how-members-of-congress-are-bribed:
Joseph H Moore, a citizen of California, addressed How Members of Congress Are Bribed to the United States Congress as an open letter, protest, and petition. Moore's target is railroad magnate Collis P Huntington. He calls Huntington the very model of a lobbyist. In Moore's account, Huntington worked Congress for nearly thirty years to enrich himself and fellow railroad men.

Moore describes threats, promises, and favors traded in corridors and offices. He argues that monopoly money had sapped honest lawmaking and harmed California's interests. Foreign parliaments, he claims, would scorn such influence. The letter asks Congress to expose and resist the railroad lobby. Readers meet a blunt piece of Gilded Age protest writing, angry at corporate power and certain that publicity is a weapon against corruption.
johnny-bear-and-other-stories-from-lives:
Johnny Bear, and Other Stories from Lives of the Hunted is a book of animal tales by Ernest Thompson Seton. Johnny Bear is a queer little cub who lives with his mother, Grumpy, in Yellowstone Park. Bears around the Fountain Hotel found the country a desirable home. A steward's order to dump kitchen garbage sets the first tale moving.

The contents also promise Tito, the story of a coyote that learned how. Tito's chapters run from captivity and her brood to a race for life. A third piece asks why the chickadee goes crazy once a year. Seton writes wild animals as real characters with habits, dangers, and families. His stories helped readers see hunted creatures as lives worth understanding.
khaled:
F. Marion Crawford, a well read American who lived much in Italy, wrote this tale of Arabia in 1891. He was the most cosmopolitan romancer of his day, at home in many lands. The tale stands in the line of the Arabian Nights, which he knew well.

Khaled is a genie, one of the jinn, who is made a man for a set span of life. He wins his change for the love of a mortal maid, and must learn what it is to be human. Pain, faith, and death teach him, in a tale told with grace and calm.
martie-the-unconquered:
Kathleen Thompson Norris set Martie, the Unconquered in Monroe, California. The tale opens on a warm, windy September day after school. Four girls drift from the post office toward the drug store.

Martie Monroe and her sister Sarah live in the shabby old Monroe house. Richer girls from the Frost and Parker homes barely know them. Norris builds her story from small town rank, slow days, and a girl who will not stay beaten. School, the post office, and the soda counter mark their small world. Small slights carry weight when a town ranks each girl by her home.
melmoth-reconciled:
Honore de Balzac wrote Melmoth Reconciled, here in Ellen Marriage's English. He gave the book to the General Baron de Pommereul. The gift honors a friendship held between their fathers and sons.

Balzac opens with a strange study of one kind of man: the cashier. Such a man sits boxed behind iron bars for hours each day. He must handle wealth all day and keep no relish for it. From that portrait, Balzac builds his Paris tale of a soul's bargain passed on. Nature, he jokes, now and then makes an honest cashier. That rare man is the hinge on which the tale turns.
miss-billy-married:
Eleanor H. Porter's sequel opens with opinions and a wedding: Bertram takes Billy in marriage. The chapters then test the young couple. Titles promise a big bad quarrel, the dinner Billy tried to get, and the dinner she actually got. Calderwell asks questions, and Billy receives advice from all sides.

Billy cultivates a comfortable indifference, tries her hand at managing, and faces enormous responsibility. Ghosts walk for Bertram before the storm clears. The final chapter is called By a Baby's Hand. Porter, identified on the title page as the author of Pollyanna, continues her comedy of a spirited wife.
narrative-of-an-expedition-into-central-:
Charles Sturt led an expedition into Central Australia in 1844 through 1846. He acted under orders from Her Majesty's Government. Both volumes sit in this one ebook file. A notice of South Australia in 1847 completes the work.

Sturt dedicated the book to Earl Grey with frank words. No land fit for settlement was found, he admits. Still, he hopes the toil was not fruitless, like his Murray voyage. Plates and maps are listed but not shown in this text. Sturt's party endured heat, thirst, and a land that defied them, and his record remains a classic of exploration.
nasa-tm-19640058418-a-feasible-approach-:
Dated June 16, 1961, Part I summarizes an ad hoc task group study run from NASA Headquarters. William A Fleming chaired the group, with Addison M Rothrock as deputy. Their subject was a practical plan for a first crewed landing on the Moon in 1967.

Part I is the summary, paired with a detailed Part II. Together they present a program plan, not a single spacecraft design. The group drew members from Headquarters, the Space Task Group, Marshall, and the Lovelace Foundation. Readers get the early case for how such a landing could be organized and timed.
nasa-tm-19660009067-preliminary-results-:
Gregory R Wichorek and Bland A Stein at Langley gave early results in Atlanta in April 1965 on a coated metal sheet for heat shields. The sheet is Ta-10W, an alloy of tantalum with tungsten. A coating protects such a metal from burning away in hot air. Langley programs were studying refractory metals, metals that endure great heat, for thermal protection systems.

High temperature oxidation tests form the core of the study. Results are called preliminary, so more work was expected. A heat shield that fails lets hot gas reach the structure beneath. Coated refractory sheet promised a reusable shield, unlike shields that burn away. The study tests that promise at bench scale first.
nasa-tm-19670002025-a-preliminary-invest:
George C. Kenyon and George G. Edwards, of NASA's Ames Research Center in California, wrote this wind-tunnel memorandum, dated March 1961 as printed. It asks whether a blunt thirteen-degree half-cone re-entry shape could be reshaped to fly and land horizontally. The basic shape's best lift-to-drag ratio was only 1.7, judged too low for a horizontal landing.

The tunnel work reshaped the rear of the cone and tested vertical surfaces, canopies, a folding extra lifting surface, control surfaces, and landing gear. Contouring the rear brought very large gains in lift-to-drag ratio without large trim problems. Flaps and elevons also helped, while a landing gear and an upper canopy caused no serious harm. One complete configuration reached a trimmed lift-to-drag ratio above six, though its behavior at high subsonic speeds still needed work.
nasa-tm-19670027093-the-electromagnetic-:
V. K. Balasubrahmanyan and E. Boldt, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this July 1967 paper with R. A. R. Palmeira, of the Southwest Center for Advanced Studies in Dallas, and G. Sandri. It studies the light given off as cosmic rays lose energy in interstellar hydrogen, the gas clouds between the stars.

The authors show that the observed temperature of hydrogen atoms in those clouds fits what cosmic ray collisions would produce. The same interactions could maintain a surprisingly high electron concentration in the clouds. Glow from hydrogen atoms excited by cosmic rays should approach, but stay below, the brightness measured from the galactic disk. X-radiation thrown off when cosmic rays knock electrons out of hydrogen atoms could directly reveal the spectrum of the rays causing the ionization. The paper recommends detailed study of these non-stellar X-rays to map low-energy cosmic rays across the disk.
nasa-tm-19670029045-the-local-supergalax:
Elihu Boldt, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in September 1967. It connects two things: the smooth background of X-rays seen across the sky, and the local supergalaxy, our neighborhood of galaxy clusters. Boldt asks whether the nearby supergalaxy leaves a pattern in that background.

He shows that Silk's model for a universal X-ray background leads to a measurable structure. The structure arises from the local supergalaxy itself. A telescope tuned to look for it would need a wide field of view and fine resolution. The expected signal, he finds, is about as strong as the observed diffuse background.
nasa-tm-19680000635-automated-data-colle:
Ralph D. Thomas, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, built measurement gear that runs itself. His report describes a fully programmable, automated system for Hall effect and resistivity measurements. Such measurements reveal how semiconductors carry electricity.

The apparatus controls all its conditions across a wide temperature span. It logs results both as typed copy and as punched paper tape a computer can read. Thomas applied it to cadmium sulfide films and to silicon samples of both conductivity types. He also explains a simple, reliable way to make electrical contacts to samples. Accuracy and calibration get their own discussion.
nasa-tm-19680023516-comparison-of-experi:
Francis C. Chenoweth and Fred W. Steffen of Lewis Research Center compare test and forecast heat values for a round ejector in this 1968 report. The ejector served a small turbojet engine with an afterburner at sea level test stands. Wall heat levels decide if the shroud can live through the hot exhaust.

Three film-cooling rules, all based on a sealed wall, gave the forecasts. The test ejector was not sealed, so the pair worked out a fix for heat lost by glow and by free air flow. With that fix, test and forecast values matched well. One rule ran low near the coolant slot and far too high near the shroud end. One more rule set wall heat equal to coolant heat, which proved too hopeful.
nasa-tm-19700032586-precritical-analysis:
Wendell Mayo of the Lewis Research Center wrote this analysis in September 1970. It looks ahead to critical tests of a small fast-spectrum reactor design. The core is ringed by molybdenum and tailored to a set power output.

A series of critical experiments was being run by Atomics International under contract to Lewis. The test materials included lithium, nitrogen, and two kinds of uranium. Refractory metals such as hafnium, tantalum, and tungsten were also used. Mayo's paper gives the calculations made before the tests turned critical. Such pre-checks keep a first critical run safe and tell staff what to expect.
nasa-tm-19710029231-liquid-oscillation-f:
Stephen Thornton and Frank Bugg of the Marshall Space Flight Center measured how liquid sloshes inside tilted tanks. Both worked in the Aero Astrodynamics Laboratory. The tanks were cylinders whose cross sections mixed a circular arc with a straight line. Shapes ran from fully round to nearly half round. Several matched tank outlines proposed for the space shuttle.

The team tilted each tank from upright to sixty degrees. They excited the liquid both along the tilt plane and across it. Then they recorded the natural sloshing frequency for each case. Slosh matters because moving fuel can push a rocket off course. Designers use such frequencies to tune baffles and control systems. The report gives the measured values shape by shape.
one-thousand-questions-in-california-agr:
Edward James Wickson compiled this farm handbook for California growers. Wickson taught horticulture at the University of California. He also edited the Pacific Rural Press in San Francisco. The foreword says the book is no systematic treatise. It arranges real questions readers actually asked the paper.

About seven hundred people sent in the questions, he says. Answers ran weekly in the paper's columns for years. Parts treat fruit, vegetables, grain, soils, and livestock. Later parts treat dairy, poultry, pests, and plant diseases. One sample asks if four feet of soil suits lemons. Wickson answers with alkali and moisture warnings. Practical farmers still gain clear, direct help here.
overruled:
Bernard Shaw prefaced his 1912 farce Overruled with an essay, The Alleviations of Monogamy. The preface alone is a small classic of Shavian provocation. The piece, he insists, is no argument for or against polygamy. It is a clinical study of how the thing occurs. Quite ordinary people, innocent of all unusual views, are its subjects.

Theorists who praise polygamy, Shaw observes, usually lead blameless family lives. The practical libertine is the opposite. He is severe on all other libertines, and wholly conventional in his professions. Sincerely so. Like the burglar crying stop thief, he defends himself as criminals plead not guilty. Society, Shaw concludes, punishes candor and then complains of falsehood. Beneath the essay sits a comedy of two couples caught in mutual infidelity.
pamela-or-virtue-rewarded:
Samuel Richardson's Pamela, or Virtue Rewarded is told entirely in letters. The hosted edition prints more than thirty of them in sequence. Pamela writes home to her parents. Her master, Mr. B., persecutes the servant girl. Her letters record each advance and each resistance. The publishers' note introduces Richardson himself before the letters begin.

Richardson was born in 1689 and died in London in 1761. He was a printer by trade. He rose to be master of the Stationers' Company. His skill as a letter-writer made him a novelist almost by accident. The note calls him the first of the great English novelists. Pamela's letters, written in the moment's heat, invented a new kind of fiction.
persia-revisited: The sample we host shows only the front matter of Persia Revisited, the title pages and the start of the contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names General Sir Thomas Edward Gordon, formerly military attaché and Oriental secretary to the British legation at Tehran. The book reports a visit in 1895, with remarks on the new shah, Mozuffer-ed-Din, and the situation in Persia in 1896. The contents begin with the road from London to Baku and its oil-wells.
phases-of-faith-or-passages-from-the-his:
Francis William Newman called Phases of Faith an egotistical book in form but not in purpose. His preface, dated March 1850, explains that friends had fallen away from him on religious grounds. He writes to show them he had no choice but to follow his intellectual conclusions, reached through learning, history, and criticism.

The book traces the progress of his creed alone, not a general autobiography. Its mighty truth, he argues, is that belief and faith are different things, and no fixed creed should test a man's spiritual character. Newman, brother of the cardinal, wrote the classic Victorian record of losing orthodoxy honestly.
pitman-s-commercial-spanish-grammar-2nd-:
C. A. Toledano wrote Pitman's Commercial Spanish Grammar, issued here in a second edition dated 1917, to teach Spanish for business use. The Pitman name marks it as part of a well-known line of commercial and shorthand manuals.

The grammar begins at the very start, with the Spanish alphabet and the sound of each letter's name. It then gives the five vowel sounds. They never vary, it says, except that stressed vowels run a little longer. Everyday words show the sounds: amigo for friend, cielo for heaven, and recibo for a receipt. From such basics the student moves toward the language of trade, the book's stated commercial purpose.
shakespeare-s-bones-the-proposal-to-disi:
C. M. Ingleby published this essay with Trubner in London in 1883. Ingleby was a life trustee of Shakespeare's Birthplace and a vice president of the Royal Society of Literature. He inscribed the essay to the mayor and corporation of Stratford-upon-Avon and to the vicar of Holy Trinity church there.

Ingleby weighs a plan to dig up Shakespeare's bones and judge what they might show about his portraits. Tales of visits by the living to the dead fill out the argument. The essay shows how fiercely Victorians guarded the poet's grave, and how far science claimed a right to look inside it.
she-stands-accused:
Victor Macclure wrote these accounts of famed women who faced the law, drawn, he states, from checked sources. He dedicated the book to Rafael Sabatini. Some women in these pages were hanged or jailed; others walked free, acquitted at least in law. An opening chapter weighs the title itself.

Macclure nearly chose a joking title about fair hands stained, then saw the trap: several women were cleared, and loose words could libel. Chapters bear heads like A Fair Neck for the Maiden and Arsenic a la Bretonne. True-crime readers get period cases told with care for the record.
sir-francis-drake-revived:
Philip Nichols set forth this account of Drake's raid on the Spanish treasure town of Nombre de Dios, drawn from reports by men who sailed with him. Drake himself reviewed the tale, a 1910 Collier printing notes, and his nephew issued it. An opening essay sketches Drake's rise.

Born in Devonshire about 1540, Drake sailed to the Spanish Main by 1565 and lost much to Spain in 1567. His 1572 venture repaid that loss at Spain's storehouse. Led by native guides to a great tree in Darien, Drake first of Englishmen saw the Pacific and prayed to sail it one day.
speeches-of-the-hon-jefferson-davis-of-m: Speeches of the Honorable Jefferson Davis of Mississippi gathers talks from the summer of 1858. John Murphy and Co. printed the book at Baltimore in 1859. The contents list a Fourth of July speech at sea. Talks at Portland and Belfast in Maine follow. A speech at the state fair at Augusta stands there. An address at Faneuil Hall, a New York speech, and words before the Mississippi legislature close the list. Davis says false reports of his talks drove him to gather them.
sugar-and-spice-comical-tales-comically-:
James Johnson's Sugar and Spice, subtitled Comical Tales Comically Dressed, came out at London from Dean and Son of Fleet Street, a firm known for Christmas cards and children's books. The tales are told in comic verse, with pictures, for young readers.

The first piece opens at a party given by children with not one grown person there. The young hosts cast lots for a servant, and the lot falls on T. Good, who will not come when rung for, will not hear when called, and must be coaxed in with marmalade to carry a letter out. His grumbling speech on how rich people treat servants gives the joke a small, sharp edge.
superseded:
May Sinclair, author of The Divine Fire, published Superseded in 1906. A publishers' note explains the reissue. Sinclair wished the book republished in America. She counted it the best of her work before The Divine Fire. It had first appeared with another work. That volume was called Two Sides of a Question.

The chapters open with a prologue, Miss Quincey Stops the Way, and close with an epilogue, The Man and the Woman.
